PATIENT MERCY JONES. • Let us venerate the bones Of patient Mercy Jones, - • • Who d lies underneath these atoll . This is her story as once told to me By him who still loved her. as all men might see— Darius, her htisband„his age seventy years, A man of few words, but, for her, many tears. Darius and Mercy were born in Vermont Both children were christened at baptismal font. In the very same place on the very same day-- (Not much acquainted just then, I dare say). . The minister sprinkled the babies, and said. " Who knows but this couple some time nia7 be wed, And I be the parson to join them tost.ther, • For weal or for woe, through ail sorts of weather !" Well, they were married, and haPPier folk Never put both their heads in the same loving yoke., They were poor, they worked hard, but nothing could try The patience of Mercy. or cloud her bright eye. She was clothed with Content as a beautiful robe; She hat „riess—who has not on this changeable globe?— But at auch times she seemed lati the sister of Job. She was patient with dogmas, where light never dawns, She was patient with people who trod on her lawns; She was patient with folks who said blue skies were gray. And dentists and oxen that pulled the wrong way; She was patient with phrases no husband should utter, She was patient with cream that declined to be butter; She was patient with buyers with nothing to pay, She was patient with talkers with nothing to say; She was patient with millers whose trade was to cozen, And grocers who counted out ten to the dozen; She Was patient with bunglers and fault-flnding churls, And tall, awkward lads who came courting hergirls ; She was patient with crockery no art could snend, And chimneys that smoked every daY the wrong end; She was patient with reapers who never would sow, And long-winded callers who never would go; She was patient with relatives when uninvited. They came, and devoured, then complained fig were slighted; She was patient with crows that got into the corn. And other dark deeds out of wantonaeas born; She was patient with lightning that burned up the hay, At She was patient with poultry nnwilling to lay; She was patient with rogues who drank cider too strong. She was patient with sermons That lasted too long; She was patient with boots that tracked up her clean floors, She was patient with peddlers and other smooth bores; She was patient with children who disobeyed rules And, to crown all the rest, she was patient with foois. The neighbouring husbands all enviect the. lot . Of Darius, and wickedly got ups plot _ • • To bring o'er his sunshine an unpleasant-spot. "You think your wife's temper is proof against fate, • But we know of something her smiles will abate.' When she gets out of etaod„ end fer more is inclined, Jest send home the erookedesi rot you can Cid Let us pick it out, letsts go and choose it, And we'll bet you a farm, when she comes for to use it, 1 Her temper will crack like Nathan Dow's cornet, And she'll be as mad as an elderly hornet.; - Darius was piqued, and fie said with a VISM, "I'll pay for the wood, if you'll send it hum; But depend on it, neighbors, no danger will come." ' Home came the gnarled roots, and a crookeker load Never entered thegate of a Christian abode. A min'4oorn 'ries straighter than any stick in ; It seemed to be wrigglingabont every minute; It would not stand up, audit would not liodown ; It twisted the vision of one-41f the town,„ Taloa at such fuel svas really a sin, For the chance was Sbismus would surely set in. Darius said nothing tndercy about it It was crooked wood—even she could not doubt it; But never a harsh word escaped her sweet lips, Any raore than if the old snags were smooth chips. She boiled with them, baked with them, washed with them through The long winter months, and none ever knew But the wood was as straight as Mehitable Draw, ' Who was straight as a die, or a gun, 02 an arrow, And who made it her business all male Hearts to harrow. When the pile was burned up, and they needed more wood, "Sure now." mused Darius, "I shall catch it good; She has kept her remarks all condensed for the Spring, ' And my ears, for the trick, now deserve well to sing. She never did scold me, but now she will pout, And say with such wood she is nearly worn out." But Merey, unruffled, was calm, like the stream That reflects back at evening.the sun's perfect beam; ' And looked at Darius, and lovingly smiled; As she made this request with a temper 'milled : • " We are wanting more fuel, lam sorry to say; I burn a great deal too much every day, ' And I mean to use less than I have in thepitst ; • But get, if you can, dear, a load like the last; I never had wood that-I liked half so well— Do see who has nice crooked fuel to sell ; Theses nothing that's better than wood full of knots, It fays so complete round-the kettles and pots. And washing and cooking are really like play -- When the sticks nestle close in so charming away." • Harper's New Monthly Magazine.

Free of charge—An empty gun. A Why is a selfish friend like 'the -letter "p"?—Reciiniet though the first in pity, he is the last in help. Never does man believe so strongly in the attraction of gravitation as when he sits down in a chair and finds it gone. We are now prepared, says the Kansas City Itmes;to re- ceive poems about "the winter's chill, bleak blast." Waste paper is worth nine cents a pound, and= stock of spring poetry has run out. The great city of Leadville was once a hamlet rude and young, and pres!,& over by a MayOr whose first proclama- tion went off in this style: "Whoever shall steal a hoes shall be hung par order of the mare!" "I have been told, doctor," said a fretful patient, troubled with insimnia, " that a man can go to sleep if he will only firmly arkl resolutely fix his mind on nothing." "Think of yourself, then," advised the doctor, bluntly. GETTING HINGS MlXED.—Scene: PaLiAll kirk in Strathendrick.—Minister (in course of his sermon) : "Cheat, rob, steal, and see what will come out ofit:"OldWoman (alp door, as congregation is dispersing): " Wha's this Rab Steel that the minister's sae doon on ?"—Neighboar "Oh. Iltat's a man that yince cheated him, an' that he disna like." —Old Woman (satisfied) : " Weel, it's a great shame o' the minister tae go on like that in the pu'pit ; shaerly he ought tae show a better example tae the folk. RELIGION AND SEcur,saa LlFE.—Religion and conduct must be harmonised in every individual, or he becomes two beings, with different faces, and pulling different ways. Such a division is fatal. You cannot split a man into two without killing him. The different sides deur nature, like the different periods of our life, should be boned each to eaah by natural piety. Work should be prayerful; prayer true ,Woric lif, a pa•.-11n.i, and praise the breath of life; for the Christian's life is love, and love Is the only all- sufficient source of happiness.—Frincipal Grant, ía "Goad Wards." "I acted Werner languidly," says. Macready in his "A circumstance in the play amused me a good deal, and at my own expense. I was inconvenienced and rather annoyed by Ulric looking on the ground, or any- where but in my face, as he should have done. My ois- pleasure, however, vanished on seeing the tsars fast trickling down his cheek, and forgiving his inaccuracy on the score elf his sensibility, I continued the scene with augmented energy and feeling, and left it with a very favourable im- pression of the young man's judgment and warm-hearted- ness. In the course of the play he accosted me' begging my pardon for his apparent inattention to me, and explain- ing the cause, viz., that he had painted his face so high on the cheek that the colour had got into his eyes, and kept them running during the whole act. What an unfortunate disclosure !" A CARPET TACC—Now, sir, let us look at a carpet tack. What is more common than a carpet tack, and yet what a remarkable lot of latent power there is in it! For years it will stay in one spot, motionless as death, and a person would not even give it a thought; but place it in the bottom of a chair and let a two-hundred-pound-man sit down on it, and what will it do? Why, sir, it will lift him up fifteen feet high and throw him the whole length of the room, and I make the house shake, his wife scream, the dogs bark, a the police come ; and yet there is not one man in a dozen who has any idea what a carpet tack can do when its power is brought into play. The keen eye of science looks beneath the surface of things, and is continually making new ceveries. Take five chairs, and in one place a tack, and the ferst Man who comes along will sit down in the chair which has the tack in it. People doubt this, but it is so, for this reason: a man is a vast magnet and constantly charged with electricity, and the tack also is electrical; thereforei.the attraction between the two is great. Dr. Richardson, in " Good Words." TRUTH BETTER 'MAN Gcmo.—Before Christmas there were prizes to be given in Willie's school, and he was very anxious to merit one of them. Willie was young, and had never hail much chance to learn, so he was behind the other boys in all his studies except writing.. As he had no hope to excel in anything but writing, he made up his mind to try for the special prize for that with all his mind. And he did try, so that his copy-book would have done honour to a boy twice his age. When the prizes were awarded, the master of the school held up two copy-books, and said, "It would be difficult to say which of these two books is better than the other, but for one copy of Willie's, which is not only superior to Charlie's, but to every other e2py ; there- fore, VVillie's book gains the prize." Willie's heart beat high with hope, which was not unmixed withlear. Blushing to his temples, he said, "Please, sir, may I see that copy ?" °Certainly," replied the master, looking somewhat surprised. WMie glanced at the copy, and, handing the book back, said, "Please, sir, that is not my writing. It was written by an upper-class boy, who took my book by mistake one day instead of his own." "Oh, oh ! ' said the master, "that may alter the case;' and after comparing them carefully, he awarded the prize to Charlie. The boys laughed at Willie. One said he was silly to say anything about the mistake. "I wouldn't have told," said another. "Nor I," added a third boy laughing. "The copy was in your book, and you had a right to enjoy the benefit of it." But in spite of all their quizzing, Willie felt that he was right. "'lt would not have been the truth." he replied, "if I had not told who wrote the copy._ I would rather hold fast the truth than have a prize, for truth is better than gold." " Hurrah for Willie! Three cheers for Willie! Well done, Willie !" - Shouted the boys, and Willie went home to his work hippier than he could have done if, by means of a silent lie, he had won the prize. ' Mess FLYNN'S LOVER.—Miss Mary Flynn was studying medicine and being courted at the same time. Mr. William .Budd was attending to the latter part of the business. One evening while they were sitting together in the parlour, Mr. Budd wee. thinking how he should manage to propose. Miss Flynn' was -explaining certain physiological' facts to him. "Do you know," she said," that thousands of persons are actually ignorant that they smell with their olfactory pen. dude ?" "Millions of Im, replied Mr. Budd. " And Aunt Mary woeldn't believe me when I told her she couldn't wink without a sphincter muscle." "How unreasonable !" "Why, a person cannot kiss without a sphincter!" "In- deed" I know it is so." " Xay I try if lean ?" "Oh, Mr- Btrld, it is too bad for you to make light of such a sub - 'feet." Then'ha tried it, and while he helrher hand she explained to him about the muscles of that portion of the human body. "It is remarkable how much you know about these things," said Mr. Budd—" really wonderful. Now. for example what is the bone at the back of the head called ?" "'Why, the occipital bone, of course." " And what are the names of the muscles of the arrds ? "-'the spiralis and the infraspiralis among others." "Well, now, let me show you what I mean. When I put my in-fra- spiralis around your waist, so, is it your occipital bone that rests upon my shoulder blade in this way?" "My hair, primarily., but the occipital bone, of course, afterwards. But oh, /dr. Budd, suppose pa should come in and see us ?" "Let him e'en. -2Who cares ?" said Mr. Budd boldly: .." I think I'll exercise a sphincter and take a kiss." "Mr. Budd, how can you ?'' said Miss Flynn, after he had performed the feat. " Don't Wipe Mr. Budd—call me Willie," he said, drawing her closer. "You accept me, don't you? I blow you do, darling." "Willie," whispered Miss Flynn, very faintly. "What, darling?" "I can hear your heart beat." "It beats only for you, my angel." "And it sounds,otit *of order. The ventricular construction is not uniform." "Small wonder for that when it's bursting for joy." "You must put yourself under treatment for it. I will give you some medicine." "It's your own property, darling; do what you like with it. But somehow the sphinctet opera- tion is one that strikes me most favourably. Let us again see how it works." But why proceed? The old, old stery ! —Troy Times. AN INCIDENT OF mu Pou...—Occasionally the figures were so close that the agents, and even the returning offi- cers, were 'wrong in their additions, and the decision of the latter had to be reversed. This occurred in 1846, when Mr. Romilly opposed Mr. Baillie Cochrane at Bridport, who had resigned his seat in consequence of the support he gave Sir Robert Peel on the repeal of the Corn Laws, and sought re- • election: On that occasion, as early as nine o'clock the numbers were equal. At ten o'clock the candidates tied again; and so on, neck and neck, throughout the day. When, at a quarter to four, 'it was supposed that Mr. Ro- milly was one in the majority, the crowd made a dash to the polling-booth; the mayor, the egents the clerks, were all swept away, and retreated into the Town Hall, where the declaration of the poll was to be made. Tif--Coniervative candidate, defeated, as he and every one supposed, demanded an interview with the mayor, to protest against the irregu- larity of closing the poll before the legal hour of four, when his worship, in a state of great confusion, requested that no .otice eltould be taken of this illegality, as the numbers had 'eon added wrong, and the majority of one was in Mr. ,Cochrane's favour. This explanation was interrupted by the enthusiastic cheers of the mob, who were going through 'ftte fuma of chairing Mr. RocaMy. So confident had his part/ been of success, that the magnificent velvet chair was ready prepared ; and.instead of adopting the usual course— of postponing the time-honoured, and, for the candidate, somewhat perilous ceremonial, to the next day—Mr. Ro- milly was compelled at once to ascend the giddy eminence, and, borne on the shoulders of eight enthusiastic and very unsteady supporters, preceded by the brass band playing "See the conquering hero comes," and followed, by a de- lighted legion of boys, stopped opposite the Town Hall to give three grateful cheers for the mayor who bad beat such a timely retreat, when suddenly his worship appeared on the balcony, claimed silence, and, to the utter confusion of the chaired, the chairmen, band, and mob, made the announce- ment that Mr. Baillie Cochrane was duly elected to serve in Parliament. It may be supposed that after this announce- ment there was a universal saure qui pest. Not a bit of it. As the story goes, the constituency was equal to the occa- sion; they were not going to be done out of their fun, so the candidates exchanged places. Arcades anibo. Mr. Romilly took his place in the chaise which was ready for the unsuccessful candidate, who did not care to be kept awake all night by the triumphant.cheers of hit rival's fol. 'lowers. Mr. Cochrane ascended the chair. The same chair- bearers continued their services, the same band played a triumphal march, the same mob cheered. The ribbons alone Were changed—the blue colours, instead of the red, fluttered in the air. It was a novelty in election experience—two Aritunphs for the same seat on the same day.—Blackwood's Magazine. REALITIES OF WALI.—War is a horrible thing in itself. The Duke of Wellington said once: "There is only one thing more dreadful than a defeat, and that is a victory •," and everybody remembers how the stern soldier sat with clenched hands and compressed lips in his tent after the battle of Waterloo, with the tears rolling down his cheeks, as the list of the British Blain was read out to him. George IV. is not usually supposed to have been a very sympathetic man; but the Countess Brownlow, in her very interesting " Recollections,"., has recorded how he wept when he saw the list of the dead. Now, it is quite true that everybody must die some day, as the Cossack commander so tenderly remarked to the Russian Empress, when she objected to a scheme for slaughtering in cold blood a few thousands of men, women, and children. But it is not true that every- body must kill; and the Cossack himself would have strenu- ously resisted the application of a naked sword to himself. Probably there is not many a soldier with a heart and con- science in his bosom, who is not sometimes haunted by the vision of some one ghastly face—the face of a brother man whom he, face to face, slew in battle. There are dreadful stories of that kind in the "Lives of Brave Soldiers." Some of the sketches which came from Woerth and Gravelotte, in the Franco-German War were almost intolerably shocking. Conceive—but who can conceive ?—a man territtly wounded, lying out in the field in a bitter frosty afternoon, anguished with thirst, unable to cry for help, or no help being near, -sild-witfi a horse's hoof every now and then crashing into his chest or his jaw. Multiply such pictures by tens of thousands. Read of the disaster of the Khyber Pass in Afghanistan in 1842, when out of 26,000 men, women, and children struggling through mountain passes in the winter, with ambushed enemies behind every crag, only one man (Dr. Brydon) escaped. We will not go on. And indeed it Is only in casual private talk with rather reckless old sol- diers or sailors that you get at the worst; it is too bad to I be printed. And then add to all this suffering, which it would be quite wrong to call merely physical, the broken hearts, the poverty, and the burdens ef debt forced upon nations by wars. Take into account the injury done to the hearts of those who never witness actual fighting. There are the-maas of mankind; they may see the flags and hear the bands of. Music and the war-cries, but they know no more; and their general character is too often injured by , sympathies which are called forth by what they hear or ' read of "war, glorious war,” Last of ail, .tet•us remember that the large majority di wars are neither'just, nor merely defensive, but are the results of some of our worst passions —those passions which we think of when we desire to form Isome conception of that place which is the opposite of ^heaven—and we have a sum total of misery sad wickedness which may well make us hate the very word battle, and cry, with aching hearts, "Lord! scatter Thou the people that delight in war !"—The Bop' Newspaper. .- '1 DEER FORESTS a. SHEEP Fannts.—" A London House- ; holder" writes as follows to The Times :—You allowed me Some time ago to question the public policy of Mr. Base in converting 42,000 acres of good Highland pasture, especially fit for sheep feeding, into a deer forest containing only a com- paratively few deer. May I, then, be permitted, on behalf of poor people like myself, to thank the Duke of Sutherland for his successful efforts to increase the number of sheep (which so many of the aristocracy are trying to diminish) by his reclamation at Kildonan and Silbrace. This is indeed a right use of property and of wealth.

feather, a good rug, and a few toilet perquisites will the outfit. Cabin requisites can be best obtained in I,Onithn, and sent by the vendor direct to the ship. They will include mattress, blankets and sheets, pillows, candles land lamp, water tin and can, screws, hooks, strips of leather and, string, nails, hammers, &c.; also soap and Eau de Cologne. A lady will require one ordinary dress of alpaca, or serge, two light coloured dresseaior the hot region,_and superior dress for Snaday. Many passengers consider alcoholic drinks essendal to an outfit.. I have not Viand them so. In case of faintness or of pain in connection with sea-sickness, I found relief In a little brandy and water, but that can be obtained from the steward. It is, indeed, easy on shipboard to acquire and to gratify a love of drink. Against such a danger it is impossible to be too firm and too vigilant. 'Nor is it necessary for a saloon passenger to bring dietetic dainties, unless determined to carry out vegetarialf principles, which in my own case have fared badly ; in fact, unless provided by yourself there is no adequate substitute for animal food. Necessity, regard to health,and the stimu- lating sea air leave no choice in the matter; but it is quite possible to lithit the indulgence to one meal a day: 5. A long voyage affords much leisure, and the old saw;'" Satan finds some mischief still for idle hands to do," is as true on sea as on land, and, we might add, true of idle, vacant minds as well. It is most important to provide plenty to do, and a variety of occupation—some form of handicraft, an ample and varied supply of books. Pre-arrange what shall be studies, and supply accordingly; say one of the modern languages, some branch of science or a work like Maury's—anything useful; improving, and absorbing; nor should light literature and music be omitted; every morn.. lug, at least, devoted to work; a worehipful eye for the glories of nature, and the society of agreeable travelling companions, will prevent ennui, and reduce the monotony of a voyage to an." unknown quantity." Since leaving "Old England" we have not once sighted land, nor are we likely to do so until our arrival at Auck- land, about (as we hope) the 15th or 16th inst., when and where I hope to add postscript and post this; we have had no chance of forwarding letters per homeward ship.—Yours faithfully, EDWIN COX.

Ship Fernglen, Oct. 4th, 1880. P.B.—Since the 4th inst., with the exception of one or two delicious days. we have had a succession of heavy gales. After passing Tasmania a strong gale from AT.E. lasted 48 hours; on the 15th we had a most severe gale from N.W., with terrific squall and high cross seas, playing havoc among the sails. Then, on the 17th, off the "Three Kings" (a group of rocks some 30 miles to the N.W. of mainland), we had I very hard, N.E. gale, with high mountaincia sea, and thick misty rain, the ship plunging heavily: We passed the "Three Kings" just before midnight on the 16th-85 days from land to land, 89 from London. Owing to hiid winds we were unable to proceed, and tacked, round, re- p3ssfng the "Three Kings' on the 19th, alidlcoming„to atchor in Auckland Harbour early on the morning of the 21st.—E. C. '

The Privy Council have directed the closing otthe cattle markets in Leicestershire This step had been taken on the representation of the magistrates that cattle disease was prevalent in the county. An Oldham pawnbroker Was, on :Wednesday, fined 10s. and coati for having refused to' supply the Statutory "form of declaration " to a woman who had lost the ticket relating to a ring which she had pledged with the defendant. The Re. Dr. Jobson, the well-&uovrn Wesleyan minister, died en Tuesday morning in London. Dr. Jebson *as president of the Cdtference in 1889, and had been a member of the "Legal Hundred" since 1853. - During the gale, on Wednesday, a steamer and a barque *ere driven on the sandbanks near Harwich. The steameri which is believed to have been a passenger boat, probably front the Continent, sank. The lifeboat went out, but could find no traces of crew or passengers. Lea EXPLOSION AT SEARAM.—The coroneft inquiry into Mei". cause of The disastrous txplosieg at Seabam, was resumed on Wednesday. Sevbral witnesses stated their belief that the colliery was well managed and ventilated; but it was admitted that on one portion of "the underground roads common paraffin lamps were used. It was believed that the explosion originated either at one of these lamps or from the use of gunpowder. "I The Liverprol steamer Brazilian, inward bound from Boston, with a cargo of grain, flour, and live stock, stranded on the Bubo Bank, at the mouth of the Mersey, shortly before two o'clock on Tuesday morning, and three-quarters of an hour afterwards she broke in two, In the afternoon ' the grain was running out of the ship's hold, but the cattle were being saved. It is thought that the Brazilian come a total wreck.

William Stanway, the hawker accused of the murder by an act of horrible cruelty, of a woman named Mellor was, on Wednesday, brought before the magistrates a‘Maccles- field and committed for trial on the capital Charge. The little girl (nine years old) Who lived with the unhappy couple; stated that whoa the prisoner called the deceased on Christmas Day he threatened that, if s'ze did nOt get up, he would bring a ved-hot poker to her. At the Derby Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday, a man named Newton, formerly an overseer of the parish of Cossall, was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment for defrauding the Midland Railway Company of £133 by sending to them an account for a Poor-rate which had never been laid. The prisoner pleaded guilty, but his "excellent character" was enlisted in his behalf, a witness balk called to show that he had been a Sunday-school teacher for 15 years. A WILD CAT.—A fine specimen of the wild cat was cap- tured last week by a rabbit catcher in one of his traps at Drysart. Seldom if ever has such a large one been secured in this district. When killed it was found to measure 3ft. in length from the muzzle to the tip of the tail, and was otherwise proportionably large, but lower set on the legs than the domesticated or house cat. The breeding of first-class shire-bred horses is making -progress in Canada. Mr. Graham lately purchased of Mr. Drew, the filly he bought at the Agricultural Hall in March last, and since his return to Canada it has been re- Bold for the large sum of £350. A letter has just been received from the gentleman named asking for the pedigree, which is as follows :—Sire, "What's Wanted," No. 2,332; dam by "Ploughboy," No. 1,745. Breeder, T. Holding, Pilling, Lancashire. He also stated that he intends to re- visit England to make further purchases of the same kind of fillies.

But to return to our voyage. The master of a sailing ship in directing his course to New Zealand knows that for motive power he may safely rely upon certain great currents of air whicb move with regularity and are as much the result of physical law as, the tides or the development of animal life; that "although the wind bloweth where it listetb," it is only seemingly capricious, that its listing and its "variables" are according to law. When, therefore, he unfurls sail in the Channel he confidently expects that Westerly gales will prevail until about 30 deg. N. latitude he enters the "Calm of Cancer" or "Horse Latitudes," beyond which the N.E. trade winds wait to fill his sails and bear him towards the equator, where he enters its belt of clouds and oppressive calm, or, as the sailors call it, "The Doldruma." Here by a collision of winds and by the intense heat a vast process of evaporation goes on, clouds are formed and heated vapour asemading high is borne by -upper cur, rents of air round the glebe, condensing upon the lofty, hills and flowing down their sides as rivulets, which gather- ing volume form great rivers and flow into the sea from whence they came. Escaping from this region he meets the S.E. trade winds-, at first as a west monsoon, because deflected by the arid desert of Africa, then as a direct steady breeze similar to the N.E. trade winds, until he enters another calm zone, the "Calm of Capricorn," or "The Variables," and through this greets the "brave westerly' or south-west passage winds, corresponding to those north of the "Calm of Cancer," by which we started, but stronger and more to be feared. For a scientific description .of thel currents of air and sea, and of the wonderful harmony and, interdependence of land and sea, clouds and climate, vapour' and vegetation, I would suggest the study of Maury's " Physical Geography of the Sea." But his description of the horrors of the "Equatorial Doldrums" refers to the ex- perience of former years, when they were crossed in a more easterly direction than now obtains. Maury states that vessels are often based two or three weeks in the "Dol- drums," that the heat is most oppressive, and that they are "a frightful graveyard on the way-side" from Europe to Australia. We crossed the equator on August 20th, in longitude 28 deg. 57.,nain. W. (wit4put .any traditional visit of Neptune), and passed throughghe Tropics ,in 20 days, averaging 2 deg. per day. During this time the heat, occa- sionally oppressive, was never intolerable; awning on poop, light attire, and usually more or less- breeze, enabled us to bear the discomfort, and beyond a sense of langour and de- bility even the delicate ones made no complaint, nor were we for a day quite becalmed. The Fernglen is at this date in latitude 44 deg. 44 S. and longitude 134,41ek. 47 E., Steadily impelled by these brave westerly wind avid, so far, the voyage has been very favourable, and the Weather ex- ceptionally fine. Nothing could surpass in pleasurable warmth or in beauty of sk% and sea some of our tropical days, and in the cooler region of the south we have had days ,of ,exceeding beauty and delicious exhilarating atmosphere. q• could 'only compare it to that which on a fine summer-- dav sweeps the summit of Snowden. We were - fortunate, .too, in starting with a good moon, for by so doing we again rejoiced in her light at the Equator, where we meet with other vessels; then ' again in this region of majestic waves and stormy winds, where we are on what our captain calls "the turnpike road," running a straight easterly course south of the Cape and Tasmania" right to New Zealand; lastly, we expect the same queenly lamp to light our arrival there. Of course," some days must be dark and dreary"—" into each cup some rain must fall." We have at times had wet, " dirty weather," cold rainy days, changeful winds, heavy and sudden squalls, " rolls" some days to every meal, intense heat, and severe cold. Once only, before reaching the southerly latitudes, on the night of September Ist, have we had a heavy thun- derstorm, when the lightning played above and around us and sat as a star or ball of fire (called St. Eltno's fire) at the top of the main-mast. This is the twelfth time Captain Bubb hes sailed this route, and he states that although we have not had the hedvy gales usual in these southerly lati- tudes, we have had unusually uncertain weather, the wind shifting without any sign ; in one instance (very excep- tional) blowinglroin the east, so heading us; and-on the afternopri of September 25th we had what is very unusual in latitude 44deg. S., a heavy thunderstorm, rain, hail, and snow descending simultaneously, the ship scudding before the kale and the lightning playing until midnight. Once, too, in this southerly region we were,taught how suddenly Our fate might have been that of the hapless Eurydice. Tuesday, Sept. 14th, was a wet, disagreeable day; the sea had a smooth, reserved, majestic energy; as we looked at it the Captain remarked-that immediately before the great tidal wave that spread destruction through the Pacific, the sea was perfectly calm. As the afternoon advanced he ex- pected more wind ; the "question is," said he "when it will come." It came as a thief in the night, about a quarter to 10 o'clock, with slight, if any, warning; the wind suddenly rose with hurricane force, and, sweeping round, struck the Fernglen on the port broadside and aft, keeling her star- board, until the bulwark and railing were under water, and driving her at the rate of 10 knots an hour. The helm refused to obey, the rain came down in a torrent, and for a few minutes there seemed a death-struggle between man and the elements. We in the saloon on the port aide were thrown violently forwards, and felt the ship did not recover herself. I At the same moment we heard the hoarse shout of the Captain, "All hands on deck," and knew there must be danger. Then we heard the mates and men rush about and labour and shout with a fierce energy as if on a battle-field, whilst the ship flew madly on. Instantly the main-top- gallant yard snapped asunder, its sail split, and with it the foresail, These minor disasters (vexing to a captain who had not had a spar broken for fifteen years) probably rescued us from a far greater. In half an hour all was over •, the moon shone still more brightly, and until,after midnight we watched the mighty waves, rejoicing that they had not that night become our tomb.

This episode emphasised the question—" Do the pleasure and possible benefit of a voyage compensate its disagree- ables, deprivations, and, it may be, sufferings and danger ?" At the end of my first week's experience I should have answered this question with an emphatic negative ; now, my reply is an equally emphatic affirmative. There is, of course, pleasure and pleasure • one man's pleasure would be another man's pain. To a robust vitality, with capacious purse and appetite, equally ready for cards or claret, cigars or cavendish, troubled neither by qualms nor by ideals, ship life may be what is called " awfully jolly." After all, life would be a poor thing, especially ship life, if it did not rise above the old Bacchanalian chorus, "Let us eat and drink, for to-morrow we die !" Given a heavy bill of disagree- ableS, deprivations, and sufferings (the dangers are prob- ably not greater than those of railway travelling), it is more than balanced- by thoSe "Diviner joys," given according as the eye is open to the wonders of Nature, and the heart receptive of its beauty and its dictates. Next to the feli- city of a pure and noble friendship, is there any higher than that inspired by the love and study of Nature ? For this study a voyage has advantages sui genera. It is one thing to get up "the winds" from Maury as a class lesson, quite another and more impressive to visit their abodes and feel their force and direction. What a vast open volume, too, is "this great and wide sea!" Its colour and its currents, its temperature and restless Constancy, its winged visitors who tirelesaly swim its surface in search, of food, its myriads of. inhabitants great and small, its vast caverns scooped out from pole to pole with their marvellous treasures of deposit ,and growth, its majesty of repose and power ever appealing to our sense of the sublime and in& nite-r-these aud other chapters—how can they be- studied but by a voyage of experiment and observation? Where, too, are the glories of sunset so dazzling and enchaining as in the Tropics? Or where do the starry host and the Queen of Heaven come forth in such brilliance and grandeur as in this samerregion ? - Or where, as on the sea, are we so im- pressed by the vastness of creation, by the mystery and om- nipotence of life? Or where so plainly see the feebleness and the pre-eminence of man? His helplessness when he confronts, his power when be obeys the laws of nature? For by obeying he tames "the ocean into our pliant bearer of burdens" and the winds into his chariot steeds. Nor is it possible with the heavens above and heart within to avoid a profound impression of that restless, must we not say intel- ligent, enero, "most hidcien, yet 'hiOst manifest," that " mystery of power" in nature, which has inspired the won- 'der and worship of men in all ages of the world. Who shalLappraise such studies and contemplations as these, or of those "quiet hours" when thought gazes within and with- out, and the past rises in smiles and tears to commune with the present, both whispering hope and courage for the future?. But "higher sentiments" apart, the addition of knowledge, imperfect, indeed, but solid, as far as it goes— krfowledge of " physkal geography" and of a new province of human life and experience, deepening our sympathy with "our sailors," and "for those in peril on the sea, with the almost invariable invigoration of enfeebled health, more than repay the disagreeables and occasional sufferings of a voyage. It would be well, I think, if every Englishman took at least one long voyage in his lifetime, and better , early than late. May I add a few siggestions, such as, in case a second I voyage awaits me, I should endeavour to follow? 1. Be- fore engaging a Passage, deal directly with the shipping cbmpttny you select; call at their head office in London or elsewhere (the New Zeiland Shipping Company's office is at 84,•Bishopgate-ktreet Within), and inspect the ship you propose to griby by.; yoUr cabin near amidships, avoid- ing the stern because of extra motion and noise of rudder and pump; and ago avoid a cabin next to a store cabin because' of its pestiferous odour. wards embraced the science of engineering under Henry Robertson Palmer, who was the founder of the lustitute of Civil Engineers. His connection with Mr. George Stephen- son, wdoin he assisted in his great Parliamentary contests, introduced him to the Lard work of the profession, and sub- sequently, in conjunction with his son, Mr. Robert Stephen- son, he took part in some of the greatest railway and other works in the early days of railways. During the latter part of his career, he was consulted by the Government con- stantly on pressing and important matters, and had practi- cally retired from every-day work. With him has gone one of the long memories which nothing escaped, and one of those counsellors and advisers from whom a valuable opinion could always be obtained. Mr. Bidder, a short time before his death, made over his beautiful seat at Ravensbury Park to his eldest 8011, the well-inown Queen's counsel, and had gone to Devonshire for good. Ia private life, there never was a more domesticated man or one more fondly attached to and naturally proad of his family. He lived to see his eldest son become one of the leading barristers of the day, and his second son a double first-class man at Oxford. In his address to the institution in 1360, in concluding his wonderful lecture on calculation, he accuses himself of irritability of temper, but those who knew him best will always bear in mind that, though somewhat brusque in manner occasionally, there never was a more staunch or true friend." During his connection with Stephenson, Mr. Bidder was sometimes required to give evidence as to rail- ways before committees of the Houses of Parliament. "What is the share capital of such a railway company ?" would be asked him, and he would reply to the question front memory. Then he would be asked for various results, involving generally half a page of figures, and he would have them ready without the use of a pencil. "How do you do it ?" a friend of mine once asked him. "I don't do it," he replied, "I see it." J. M., Prescot. _ FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

div.head: FRANCE AND THE VATICAN..
div.p: FRANCE AND THE VATICAN..
- _ A telegram from Rome states that the Pope has decided to "reestablish" friendly relations with France, M. Deprez having given satisfactory assurances. AFGHANISTAN. . . •

Tranquility appears to prevail over nearly the whole of Afghanistan. Despatches from Candahar state that the country was never more prosperous, and that to all outward appearance the people are contented; but the correspondent of the Times rather naively adds that "it is very possible that this is mainly due to the general impression that pre- vails that we are about to leave the country in the spring." Military opinion on the spot is nearly unanimous in favour of retaining Southern Afghanistan. A Calcutta despatch admits that it is difficult to obtain trustworthy news regard- ing the state of affairs at Cabul, but asserts that it is beyond doubt that Abdurrahman is ruling with some severity and raising what revenue he can by forced loans or otherwise. The Civil and Military Gazette of Lahore states that arrangements for the future security of the Khyber line have been made between the Commissioner of Peshawar and the Jirgahs of the Pass and the Afreedees. The tribes are to maintain a guard of 100 men at Ali Musjid and the same number at Jarnrood. These men are to be in the pay of the British Government, and their duties are to be the fur- nishing of escorts twice weekly between Jamrood and Dakka. The tribes heretofore in the receipt' of "allow- ances" from the British Government are to continue to receive them, and the British garrisons are to be withdrawn from Ali Musjid, Lundi Kotal, and Dakka. Fifteen days are to be allowed to complete the arrangements. It is added that the turbulent tribe of Zakha Khels was not represented in the Jirgahs, and, therefore, is not bound by the engage- ments. No official confirmation of this has been made public. • THE WAR IN THE TRANSVAAL. SPREAD OF THE RISING.-INTENSE EXCITEMENT. . -

CAPI3 Toww, Dec. 30th.—The news from the Free States is very serious. The excitement amongst the Dutch popu- lation here is intense, and it is reported from Bloemfontein that should troops be despatched from England to fight against the Boers of the Transvaal the people will insist upon making common caun6with the latter. It is needless to say that the participatiorr in the war of the Free States would not only add to the difficulty of our task in the Transvaal, but would render the position of our forces in Basutoland most precarious. The report that great excite- ment prevailed in the Orange Free State is confirmed. It is stated that President Brand has declared that he will be unable to restrain the Boers of the State from joining bands n itla the Tratisvaalers. The position of Colonel Bellairs and his small force is regarded as extremely hazardous. The troopship Euphrates, which leaves Bombay on the 11th inst.; with reinforcements for Natal, will call on her way at Ceylon, and there embark 300 men of the 102nd Regiment, who have also been ordered to Durban to rein- force the troops now being sent to the Transvaal. DURBAN, Dec. 31.—The Boer version of Transvaal affairs received at Cape Town says that the Republican Volksraad placed the Government in the hands of the Triumvirate already reported, who have dec:ared a Republic. A state of seige is expected. The British supplies at Potchefstroom will soon fail. The Boers say they sent a letter to the com- mander of the British troops marching from Leydenburg to Pretoria forbidding the advance. The officer gave orders to move on, and Joubert then ordered the Boers to charge. "Within 130 yards," he says, "we charged, dismounted, and fired. A capitulation followed. It was only a matter of fifteen minutes." The wounded were sent to Pretoria. Over fifty were killed, and the rest made prisoners. The war excitement in the Free State is very great. In the Cape Colony the revolt is regarded as a terrible calamity. It is hoped that reinforcements will be speedily forthcoming. The military authorities do not deem it advisable to denude Cape Town of its garrison. Sir G. Colley has issued an ad- mirable address to the troops, in which he says that the stain cast on our arms must be quickly effaced, and the rebellion must be put down; but the Major-General trusts that officers and men will not allow the soldierly spirit which prompts them to gallant action to degenerate into a feeling of revenge. The task now forced en us by the un- provoked action of the Boers is a painful one under any cir- cumstances, and the General calls on all ranks to assist him in his endeavours to mitigate the sufferings it must entail. We must be careful to avoid punishing the innocent for the guilty, and must remember that, though misled and delnded, the Boers are in the main a brave and high-spirited people, and are actuated by feelings that are entitled to our respect. Wakerstroom is not taken. The Loyalists are "trekking" into Natal. The troops now en route are about 1,500 in number, including two guns and a Gatling battery. Sir G. Colley starts to-morrow. THE ATTACK ON THE 94TH REGIMENT.

Some highly interesting details 'of the 'attack upon the detachment of the 94th by the Boers, are to hand. Captain Lambert, of the 21st, has arrived at Pietmaritzburg. He states that the detachment of the 94th were in charge of a convoy, and necessarily straggling over a large extent of country, when a peremptory summons to surrender was addressed to the Colonel. That gallant officer had "two minutes'" grace given to him, but he scorned to debate the proposal for a moment, and attempted to place his men in a position to resist. Immediately fire was opened on the men from "all the hills around "—the ambuscade had been well planned—and in a few minutes upwards of 100 were struck down, with nearly all their officers. The Colonel then gave the order to cease resistance, and the Boer " victory" was complete. The affair was not a battle but a massacre, the summons to surrender having been merely a ruse to save appearances. The Boers have given further proof of the treachery of some at least of them by shooting Paymaster Elliott, of the 94th, when be was unharmed and a prisoner in their hands. Captain Lambert states that on his way • from Heidelberg to Pietmaritzburg he met large numbers of Boers coming in from the Orange Free State to the assis- tance of the Transvaalgs. He estimates their force at Heillleberg alone at 8,000 men. The vigour and audacity of the Boer leaders is further shown by their invasion of Natal. They have pushed a corps across the front, and talen up a strong position on the difficult road which .Sir G. P. Colley must pass over with the reinforcements he has gathered. Should the Boers be in strong force, it is probable that Sir George will be compelled to wait for further rein- forcements, and in that cage it must go hard with the feeble garrisons in the Transvaal.

AMERICA. It is stated that out of a total revenue in 1880 of MO millions of dollars the Customs receipts at the Uniteffi States ports yielded no less than 200 millions and the Inland Revenue taxes 131 millions. The office of Secretary of State in General Garfield's Cabinet will, it is expected, be offered to Senator Blaine, who was one of the candidates for the nominatioeat Chicago. THE GREEK DIFFICULTY. ARBITRATION DECLARED. GREECE ARMING AND THE PORTE PROTESTING. The Porte having, it is said, declined to submit to arbitra- tion, and the Greek Parliament having passed the loan bill for 120,000,000 of drachmas, fears are entertained that the Greeks will shortly commence hostilities. It is reported that France and Germany will try mediation. The Porte has telegraphed instructions to its representa- tives abroad explaining its objections to the arbitration pro- posal. As the proposal was not formally made in writing an oral reply is considered to be sufficient.

, Information has reached the Porte that Greece is intro- ducing quantities of arms on the main land from Corfu and Santamanra, and preparing a descent of volunteers. Foreign vessels are employed in these proceedings. The Porte pro- poses to call the attention of the Powers to this manifest vio- lation of the treaties guaranteeing the perpetual neutrality of the lonian Islands. The frontier is also harrassed by military bands. Instructions have been forwarded to the French Ambassador at Athens to protest energeticillyagainst the menacing attitude of Greece. If France, as the spokes- man -of the Powers, should declare that they would not intetfere between the combatants should Greece not obey, paeific counsels would instantly Prevail, since the Turkish Fleet would have the enemy at its mercy in forty-eight hours. CoitsTArrriNoryt, Jan.. VEvening.—The Porte has des- patched a Note to the Powers on the Hellenic question, in which it brings forward arguments against arisitratiou, and Proposes that a meeting of delegates of the Powers, iqcluding Turkey and Greece should be held at Constantinople for the purpose of fixing die Turco-Greek frontier. PARIS, JAN. 3.—A telegram from Vienna says it is be. lived that, notwithstanding the 'refusal of the Porte to accept arbitration the Powers will renew their efforts in Constantinople an'd Athenstobring about apacefic settlement of the Turko-Greek frontier question, and so prevent a con- flict the consequence of which would be incalculable both tO Turks and Greece. There are two slightly reassuring items in the news from the East of Europe. The Porte fiuds, as was anticipated, that it cannot "send 100,000 men to the frontier" without , ,

funds, and funds it has none. The produce of the Govern- ment copper 'nines is to be hypothecated in order to pay for the transport of the troops. Again, the Greek Premier does not appear now to be. so sternly opposed ato al bitration as he has been. He has requested to be informed, before giving a definitive answer' of the basis en which the Powers intend to proceed. The Powers are using great diplomatic pressure at Athens and Constantinople to avert an actual outbreak of hostili ties. The latest news from the East tends, although slightly, to strengthen the hope that the arbitration proposal would, after all, be accepted. Both from Athens and Constantino- ple we learn that the refusal to accept arbitration grows less and less decided. The Greek newspapers express great sur- prise at ths acceptance of the proposal by England, which Power they had regarded as being decisively committed to the frontier suggested by the Berlin Conference. Public opinion in Greece is still said to be insuperably opposed to the scheme of arbitration, but the Powers continue to in- sist very strongly on the absolute necessity of adoptirg it. The Greek. Government intimates that although the decree summoning the reservists to arms has been ptepared, it will not be issued for several weeks. A telegram from Constan- tinople says that the Note addressed by France to Greece declares that the decision of the Berlin Conference upon the question of the Turco-Greek frontier did not constitute a warrant for seizing the territory concerned, and conse- quently it throws the whole responsibility for the war that threatens upon Greece, which must hear the brunt alone. THE WAR BETWEEN CHILI AND PERU.

A telegram from Santiago de Chili reports an engage- ment in the harbour of Callao, between the Chilian iron- dads and the Peruvian torpedo launches. The Huascar en- gaged the shore batteries, and afforded the Peruvians an op- portunity of witnessing the effect of their own guns turned against themselves.

that would show the character of the Meetirgs held in different districts under the auspices of the Laud League.' They hoped, however, that counsel for the traversers would not take advantage of this decision and introduce irrelevant nutter. A speech of Mr. O'Shaughnessy, at Limerick, in which he recommended a peaceful settlement of the land question, was read. In the course of the proceedings Mr. M‘Donogli, one of the defending counsel, professed his per- fect confidence in the tribunal before which he appe 'red. A large body of evidence was given by shorthand writers of speeches made by the traversers in various parts of the country. The evidence given on Tuesday in the trial which is now proceeding in the Court of Queen's Beech, at Dublin, was almost entirely that of shorthand writers who had been en- gaged to attend meetings of the Land League for the purpre of taking notes of the speeches. One of them, Mr. Curtis, of London, specially engaged, deposed to the violent utterances of Mr. -Dillon sod others at Bellaghadereen. The language of Mr. Parnell, M.P., Mr. Boyton, and others of the traversers was declared by two members of the Irish Con- stabulary who have a knowledge of shorthand, and who, on account of the unwillingness of Irish press men to expose themselves to obloquy, had, in the capacity of reporters, at- tended and takes imperfect notes of the speeches at several meetings. One of the witnesses, Jeremiah Stringer, was under examination when the Court adjourned for the day. At the trial of Mr. Parnell, M.P., and others in Dublin, on 'Wedcesday, the evidence of shorthand writers as to the language indulged in by the defendants at various land meetings was continued. The speeches were of the same general tenor as those quoted on previous days, except Unit, perhaps, the epithets used by thetraversers in speaking of the landlords were stronger and more offensive. Mr. Bovton and others advised that any man taking a farm from which another had been evicted should be " visited with the severest sentence of social ostracism "—a form of punish- ment now known as Boycotting—and Mr. Nally, at one meeting which he attended, told the people to buy "doctor's pills" (meaning bullets) in preference to whisky. The people were 080 tpld that licence to carry rifles could be procured for 10s. ap;ece, and with these they might practice the shooting of vermin. The trial was again adjourned. The Land League trial in Dublin proceeded on Thursday, in the absence of several of the traversers, who, being mem- bers of Parliathent, had gone to London in order to be in their places on the opening night of the session. Whether this was with the direct sanction of the Court does not ap- pear, but as the learned judges took no note of the absence of the principal defendants it may be assumed that it had, at any rate, their tacit approval. The evidence was of the same general character as that given on several preceding days, the witnesses examined being members of the Irish constabulary who, having some knowledge of shorthand, had attended various land meetings in the capacity of Govern- ment reporters. The Attorney General put in a number of copies of the Naiim., which gave an account of therise of the Land League and the establishment of branches in various parts of the country. The trial was again adjourned. In reply to a question as to whether the Court would sit on Saturday Mr. Justice Fitzgerald said that that depended upon the progress made in the meantime. Mr. Parnell, M.P., left Mitolin on Wednesday morning for London, to be present at the opening of Parliament, and several of the other traversers, who are also members of Parliament, took their departure later in the day.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TwunsnaT, The second session of the tenth Parliament ;of the present reign was opened by Royal Commission. Owing to the absence of the Sovereign, the proceedings were merely of a formal character. About 50 ladies occupied seats on the Opposition benches, and there were only a few visitors in the Peeresses' Gallery. The Strangers' Gallery was, however, well filled within a few mil-lutes of the commencement of the proceedings. At two o'clock the Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack, and directly afterwards took his place with the' Commissioners on a bench in front of the Throne which as usual on these occasions was undraped. The ',Ord Chan- callor having desired the Usher of the Black Rod to desire the attendance of the House of Commons to hear the Royal Commission read, that officer at once proceeded to the other Chamber, and shortly afterwards the Speaker, attended by a crowd of members of the House of Commons, appeared at the Bar. After the reading of the Royal Commission by the Clerk at the Table,

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

A MAN SHOT AT His OWN DOOR—On Saturday night a man called at the house of a labourer named Patrick Dinan, in Blackpool, in the city of Cork, and inquired for Dinan. The latter came out to the door, and a conversation occurred, a few words of which only were overheard by the inmates. The stranger asked Dinan had he been to the Custom House. Dinan made a reply which was inaudible. The conversation went on for a few seconds, when a shot was fired. The inmates of the house rushed out, and found Dirndl leaning against the wall in the passage. He had been shot in the right side, just above the collar bone. The stranger had disappeared. Dinan refused to make any state- ment whatever, and desired that no instructions should be given to the police. Shortly afterwards the wounded man was taken to the infirmary, and in answer to the questions of the physicians declined to say how he had received the wound. He would rather be torn in pieces than say any- thing. The resident magistrate, Mr. Mitchell, could elicit nothing. Any information the police have was obtained from the inmates of the house. The latter was unable to describe the stranger, it being dark when he came. The police say it is a Fenian outrage. The Custom House is known to be the name given to a certain Fenian rendezvous near the lough. The latest statement made by Dinan is that ha knows who fired the shot, but will not give his name. The police are searching for the second bullet OR the premises of the injured man. The slight hemorrhage from the wounds leads the surgeon to suspect an injury in the lung. A DEMONSTRATION STOPPED.—The Clondalkin meeting, which was to take place on Sunday evening outside Dublin, was proclaimed. Of course the proclamation set forth the date. In order not to come into contact with the police. it Was decided to hold the meeting on Saturday, when Mee,-s. Davitt and Healey, M.P., were to attend. Being a holiday, a large number of country people attended. A procession of tradespeople went through the !own, headed by bands and a break, in which were seated Messrs. D ivitt an 3 llealy,M.P., with clergymen, merchants, &c. All marched to the Mall, where Father 114‘Kee parish priest of Y.anasterboic, was ap- pointed chairman, Mr. James K. Drew, P.L.G.,proposed, and Mr. P. Green, T.C., eeconded the first resolution. Mr. Davitt made a stirring speech, and Mr. Healy then came forward. At this mbment Messrs. Keogh and Lloyd, resident magistrates, came through the crowd and called on the chair- man to stop the meeting. The chairman asked for their au- thority. They replied they had none, and would give none, but if the people did not disperse at once they should use force. All dispersed after Mr. Healy addressed to them a few words. The police were present, and reinforcements were hurried in from the country. Ten thousand people were present. The Riot Act was read by Mr. Lloyd to cause the quiet dispersing of the people, but all was peaceable. All the people dispersed quietly, and the town ssttled down to its usual normal state.

A lICLIMAN IMPRISONED.-At the petty sessions. Limerick, a well-known character named Connors, alias Norry Darling, was prosecuted on a char^ of interfering with the sale of the hunters belonging to Captain Stacpoole, master and owner of the Clare harriers, at the horse reposi- tory of Mr. Hartigan, of Upper Cecil-street. "Norry" WAS employed to stop the sale by going through the city as bell- man and warning all parties, under pains, penalties, and threats, not to attend the sale or dare to make bids for any of the animals belonging to Mr. Stacpoole. Some few gentle- men attended at the repository, but it was found impossible to have a satisfactory sale, and it was adjourned. Evidence having been given, the bench decided ,on giving Norry Dar- ling three months' imprisonment with hard labour, with an intimation of regret that the term of imprisonment for such a vile act could not be doubled. Several gentlemen said the real offenders were laughing outside the dock, and that Con- nors was only the scapegoat who had to bear the odium of their dasterdlv conduct.. . . -

Mr. Mitchell Henry, in a letter to the Radical League, formed to support the Government in their policy towards Ireland, expresses his belief that the present Government will do full justice to the Irish tenant. He points out that the present agitation has unhinged society completely, and he doubts whether since the French revolution there was ever such a reign of terror as now exists in Ireland. He be- lieves that a just settlement of the land question would not satisfy the extreme men, who are fattening on the agitation and Secretly urging on poor ignorant men to dangers which they themselves will not share. He says he has received numerous letters from influential priests and laymen lamen- ting that truth and honesty are banished from Ireland. , t On Tubsday, an iron but warrconveyed to Mr. O'Donnell's farm, where the herds have been "Boycotted." It was escorted from Athlone by a troop of dragoons. A large force of police was delipatched ti HollymOunt on Tuesday to'prO- tect process servers. &Me men of the Army Service Corps, with ambulances and an iron hut, started on Tuesday for ICilbree Westport, guarded by dragoons. A strong party of police left Castle- bar for the same place at an early hour. An offer of £5OO reward is made in the Dublin Gazette by the Lord Lieutenant to any person or persons who shall within six months give information leading to the Conviction of the person or persons who fired at Canon Fleming. THE MURDER OP LORD MOUNTMORRPS.—Three of the prisoners charged with the murder of Lord Mountmorres were brought up at Clonbur Courthouse on Tuesday, and remanded until Tuesday next at Galway. The prisoner Hanberry could not be brought from the barrack, as he is suffering from a fracture of the skull. David Graham, otenant farmer, who recently eh( t dead a bailiff named Mulholland, was tried at the Omagh Assizes for murder. He was convicted of manslaughter, and was sentenced to penal servitude for life. In connection with the attempt to murder a non-union stonemason at Cork, the police on Tuesday apprehended a man named O'Brien, who was identified by the injured man as one of his assailants. Mr. Chitty, M.P., spekking at Oxford en Tuesday evening, • said with reference to Iteland that the suspension of the Habeas Corpus Act would not suffice. The removal of this safeguard of personal freedom would enable the Government to pick off the leaders in the agitation, but they could not imprison the masses of the people. Remedial measures should go hand in hand with coercion. What we should pro- bably see was the reintroduction of some of the provisions of the Peace Preservation Act and the Westmeath Act, and a land measure proceeding on the lines of the Act of 1870. It is officially announced that the Government; being con- vinced that the military force now in Ireland is sufficientiecie meet any emergency, does nut ptppose tolencl ang fart** reinforcements. There are now in Ireland 26 battalions of infantry, with a total establishment Of 17,000 men, the largest number which has. over been quartered in that coun- try. Sir Thomas Steele, the commander-in-chief in Ireland, has also at his command seven regiments of cafidrjr, and his whole force is set down at about 25,000. men, reckoning the headquarter and depot staffs and the marines,* , ham M.P.'s ASKED TO RESION.—At a Land League Meeting at Bandon, on Tuesday, a resolution was proposed asking Messrs. Shaw-and Colthurst to resign their seats for cbunty -Cork; their opinions not being in consonance with. those of their constituents; but it was Afterwards modified into one requestiog them to sit wikh thi advanced Home Rulers. .

They used such violence that the man sustained concussion of the spine an a severe shock to the system. Colonel Ring-Harman, being waited upon by a large number of his tenantry who asked for a reduction of 25 per cent, in their rents, spoke warmly to them of their" unrea- sonableness and ingratitude." He told them that his rental was £2,000 below Griffith's valuation, that the tenants Weie treated with the greatest leniency and even generosity, and that he would not give way to intimidation and threats. "When such are used," said Colonel King-Harman, "I must courageously put my UWE to the wall.", 'fle added that God only knew how he had worked for the good of his jioiirs feliantry. He had expended energy, money, time, and grin in trying to befriend them, and whit had been his reward? Any paid adventurer could get up at a public meeting and -call him any name he liked. This rebuke- elicited- the remark from somebody that. they "could not • prevent a voice- in a crowd saying things." , The tenantry were afterwardarnet by Land League agents an 4 "directed". ,to "hold their money unless they got their demand." div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

WAO,S IN THE Currox TRADE.—Ata meetingof spinners held at Blackburn on Thursday evening it was resolved to seek a meeting with the Employers' Committee with a view to making application foran advance of wages. YORKSHIRE Coal. TRADE.—A special meeting of South Yorkshire and North Derbyshire representatives was held at B irnsley, on Monday, to consider the replies from the miners' lodges respecting a demand for 10 per cent. advance. The replies generally confirmed the executives' resolution to make the demand. MINERS' WAGS IN WEST LANCASHIRE.—The fortnight's notice given by the miners of West Lancashire for an ad- vance of wages equal to the last reduction expires on Mon- day next; and the position of affairs was the _subject of a discussion at a meeting of delegates held on Monday at the Miners' Hall, Wigan- A resolution was passed appointing a deputation to seek an interview with representatives of the employers, and efforts are being made to arrange for a con- ference this week. A GREAT STRIKE or "COLLIERS has. been entered upon in the Bolton district, the object being to procure the carrying out of the Employers' Liability Act in its cntiretv. The men refuse to have an assurance system as a substitute for the compensation provided by the Act, and about 4,000 of 'them have come out on strike. On Wednesday a num- ber of the men .on strike in the Worsley district ranged themselves under a leader and in their progress through the district behaved themselves in a lawless manner. WAGE IN THE IRON TRADE—On Monday, the new scale reducing ironworkers' wages came into operation in Stafford- shire. At some of the works the men refused to resume. Later in the day a section of them, yielding to the persua- sions of operative members of the Wages Board withdrew their refusal. Others remained obstinate, and the works where they are employed are standing. In other cases the men have resumed upon the understanding that the ques- tion of the reduction shall quickly come again before the Board. STRIKE OF IRONWORKERS AT BILSTON. On Tuesday there was a crowded meeting at Bilston of ironworkers on strike against the 3d. per ton drop in wages ordered by the Staffordshire Conciliation Board. The speakers said the puddlers could not live on 7s. 3d. per ton. They urged that the sliding scale worked against them. A motion to "play on" was received with marked favour, and passed by a large majority over an amendment counselling the re-summoning of the Conciliatory Board. Ihe works in the Bilston dis- trict therefore remain idle. RAILWAY SERVANTS AND THE HOURS OF LABOUR.—At a meeting of railway employes held in this city, on Sunday afternoon, the following proposal as to hours of working was submitted :—Pointsmen, signalmen, and switchmen, eight hours per day; enginemen, drivers, firemen, guards, shunters and yardmen, nine hours (or 120 miles ffti engine- men and 150 for passenger trains); stationmen, platelayers, draymen, kc., ten hours; all overtime to be paid for at the rate of one and a quarter above the ordinary pay. This proposal was unanimously accepted, and it was resolved to press for its adoption by the different co-aipanies. STRIKE OF RAILWAY PORTERS AT BLACKBURN.—A dis- pute as to the hours of labour has resulted in all the goods I porters at Blackburn railway station, numbering 180, being thrown out of employment. Failing to obtain a reduction of hours from 11 to .10 per day, they resolved to refuse to work overtime. They were informed they must work over- time or be paid off. They left work, and an application to be allowed to resume was refused. Porters were brought from neighbouring towns to carry on the work temporarily. ' A number of new hands have also been engaged, and the whole of the places of the old staff are being filled up. WACiES IN THE COTTON TRADE.-011 Tuesday Mr. Wat- son, secretary to the Blackburn Cotton Spinners and Mann-. facturer' Association, received a letter from Mr. Cocking, secretary to the Card and Blowing Room Hands' Associa- tion, stating that it had been resolved to give notice to the Employers' Committee that on and after the 22nd inst., the operatives would require an advance of 5 per cent, on their present rate of wages, the members being strongly of opinion that the time had arrived when another instalment of what was taken from them in 1878 ought to be restored, con- sidering the improvement of trade since they received the last advance of 5 per cent. PROBABLE STRIKE OF COLLIERS IN THE ASHTON AND Otrarear DISTRICTS.—The Oldham, Ashton, and District Miners' Association recently proposed to accept arbitration, as offered by the -masters, provided such arbitration was confined to the consideration of prices paid in 1869. This condition the Masters' Association have not accepted, and at their meeting kold on Tuesday, at the Albion Hotel Manchester, it was resolved unanimously: "That this Association absolutely declines the proposal submitted on behalf a the miners to refer the question of wages to arbi- tration on the limited basis of the prices paid in 18(39; but the Association We've deeded to adjourn -the. meeting to Tuesday next, at 3-30 p.m., when any amended proposal will be received arid considered." THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES:A stronger tone has been noticeable in the iron trade of this district during the past week, and although buyers want very little iron for present requirements there is considerable ;inquiry for forward delivery. Sellers, however, are exceedingly cautious about committing themselves very far forward, and in some cases higher prices have been asked, but any very material upward movement in values tends to check busi- ness. North country irons are dearer than last week, but quotations for these are little more than nominal. In the finished iron trade there has been a firmer tone, and al- though bars are still to be bought at as low as £5 17s. 6r, . delivery into the Manchester.. district/ it is exceptional Where makersaire now quoting under .£6 per ton.—There has not heel 'very much doing in the coal trade of this dis- trict during the past week. Prices nominally are about the same as last week, the average quotation for best coal at tbe pit mouth being about Os; for seconds,. 7s to 7s ed; 'corn-' mon house coals, 6s to 6s Gil • and steam and forge coals, 5s 3d to 5s Gd per ton. There has been a good deal of pres- sure for engine classenif "ftelr'Snir'as" there is rather a scarcity of 'good qualiei of slaok offering in the market, prices have shown an trfitard tendency, and in some cases advances of 3d. and 6d. per ton upon late rates are being asked, the better descriptions of slack at the pit mouth be- ing now qqoted at from 38 3d to 3s 01 per ton, with good burgy averaging about 4s 3d to 4s 9d per ton.

div.head: WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: WATER COMMITTEE.

Aid. GAMBLE propos.d the confirmation of the minutes of the Water Committee, which contained the following : " The Chairman submitted and read proposed heads of terms which he and the Deputy-Chairman had proposed for submission to Lord Derby, for approval, on the subject of the contemplated supply of water to the St. Helens district, from his lordships estate at Knowsley." At the request of Aid. Johnson, Aid GAMBLE read over the terms, which he requested the reporters not to publish. Mr. BROOK: Why has water been refused to the Lanca- shire Chemical Company? Aid. GAMBLE said the works were not near the mains, and there would be difficulty in supplying them. The minutes were confirmed.

GAS APPARATTS. Mr. T. COOK Moved the confirmation of the Gas Como mittee's mutes, whith contained the following :—" Re- solved that the following apparatus be obtained for use at these works-Ist, for illuminating pviver. photometer, dm, £46 17s. 01. ; 2nd, ammonia test, £4 Os.; 3rd, •ulphur test, £39 17s. id.; 4th, sulphuretted hydrogen test, £2los. ; total, £93 10s. 71. Resolved that one of Livsev's patent washers be obtained, for these works, at a cost of £l2O. It was re- solved that the tender of Godel Waizborn, for the erection of laboratory, testing room, and office, in the gas works yard, according to the plan and specifications, for the sum of £5B 10s., be accepted, the Corporation to supply bricks and mortar."

1- Mr. ALLEN asked how it was there had been such a defec- tive illumination of the gas? Mr. COOK said the low illuminating power bad not es- caped the attention of the committee, and he had com- plained personally to Mr. Hall about it. They had been getting inferior coal lately, and one of the hydraulic mains burst, which ,2aused air to get in. In answer to Aid. Gam- ble, Mr. Cook confessed that he was puzzled with Mr. Hall's book, in reference to the illuminating power of the gas. Aid. GAMBLE: My impression is that the illuminating power is not two-thirds of that stated in the minutes, 18 45 candles. The minutes were confirmed.

THE BATHS.—ST. HELENS CHEMICAL COMPANY.—NIGHT SOIL • FOREMAN. Dr. Tav-vronn proposed the confirmation of the minutes of the Health Committee, and this was seconded. Mr. BROOK asked why the committee had decided to close the baths with the exception of two days in the week. Dr. TWYFORD explained that they found very few people attending the baths except on those two days, and by clos- ing them they saved 203. a week. Aldermen Johnson drew attention to the report of the Medical Officer on the dreadful state of the atmosphere. The doctor said, "I have had special complaints from parties residing near the St. Helens chemical works. Iberia remonstrated with the manager of the works, and he has ' promised to abate this nuisance, but last week the evil still existed." He (Alderman Johnsop) had b?en spoken to by a person connected with the worW, and he was told that the naisance did not proceed from those works, but from some chimneys close to. Mr. FOSTER: I should like te ask bow it is the com- mittee could not select a foreman of the nightsoil depart- ment frotmthose who 1i3,33 in the town and who applied. I should like to know 'why we had to go to Manchester for I ft man who is a stranger to the town and knows nothing about the work. Mr. T. Coos: Was not Mr. Foster at the meeting. Dr. TWYFORD: He was at the meeting. Mr. Fosren.: But I opposed what was done. I ask the Council because I did not know why they selected the Man- chester man in preference to a St. Helens man.

..... Dr. TWTFORD 6:lid there were 130 applications, and sir candidetes were selected, among whom were two St. Helens men. He supposed they selected the best man. He had been accustomed to have the control of men. •

... ~. —...- Mr. McKEemorta : It so happened that Mr. Foster and I voted for a townsman, and our chairman voted for another, but the mljority ruled against a wise selection. But m 14% °d ul doubt they made . . -- M. Foster has the satisfaction of having done hu!, duty with others. I Ibt minutes were confirmed. '

FLANS.—CHURCH OF THE SACRED HEART. Alderman JonNsoN moved, and Mr. BELSHER seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of the Health Committee, which contained the following :—",The matter of the charge for paving, &e., made by the corporation in respect of the frontage of land adjoining the:Church qf the Sacred Heart to Banner, Reilly, and Manning-streets, again considered. The Chairman having stated that the land referred to was in reality the churchyard, and had been consecrated as such, it was resolved that the charge be not pressed if the bishop, Dr. O'Reilly will give to the corporation an undertaking Main case any building or buildings other than a church, chapel or meeting house, consecrated, licensed or certified as mentioned in secthin I(ks of the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1e169, be erected at time hereafter on the site of the said piece of land; lirot his soccessors, as the case may be, will pay to the corporation such proportionate charge for paving, itc ,the said streets, in respect of the frontage of any such blinding or buildings as the owner of any such building or buildings would he liable to pay, if the same had been erected when the pavement, &a., was executed." Alderman GAMBLE reminded the town clerk to embody the above resolution in the undertaking. Mr. Balms said it should have his attention. _ Alderdnin (*AMBLE asked if all the plans submitted at the last meeting of the Paving Committee were in accordance 'with the Act and bye-laws of the corporation. It appeared there had been some misunderstanding as to the meaning of the clause of the Act, and the clauses in the bye-laws in re- gard to the fixing of the backyard space. Therefore he wished to ask the chairman if the plans were in accordance with the clauses, and if measures had been taken to insure that all plans conform with the bye-laws. Alderman JOHNSON : So far as I am able to judge these plans are in accordance with the bye-laws, and there was a special resolution passed at the same time calling the atten- tion of the surveyor to them in the future.. The minutes were confirmed.

labours of the law makers will be even more than usually arduous. The plan of the last Government of crowding the table of the House with Bills, and failing to pass them, is not to be followed by the present Government, who evidently intend to attempt to pass a few good and neces- sary acts rather than endeavour to run through a large grove of bills and miss their mark. A proposal will be made for the abolition of flogging in the army and navy. An attempt is to be made to effect a change in the bankruptcy law, and to give greater protection to creditors over debtors' estates. Farmers and others will hail the promise that something is to be done to promote the conservance of rivers and the prevention of floods. A revision of the con- stitution of the endowed schools and hospitals in Scotland is to be effected; and as the Ballot Act will have to be renewed, and as cognisance is taken in the Speech of the corrupt practices which prevailed in certain towns at the last general election, important ohanges will be effected in that statute.

IsTzw YEAa's DIY AT RUNCORN.—This day was scarcely observed at all in Runcorn, as it fell upon a Satur- day. Most of the places of business were, however, closed on Monday, and numbers left for Liverpool and neighbour- ingtowns. INTEREBTEM SERVICE AT RATON YARIBIE CHURCH. —On New Year's Eve a special service was held in this Parish Church, which was beautifully decorated. Imme- diately before midnight, those present were requested to spend a few minutes in private prayer. The bell was tolled as the old year went out to join the years that have been, and the vicar then stepped down from the pulpit, shook hands with each present, and wished him or her "A happy new year." The sermon was upon "We bring our years to an end."__
