Ma new num Aim THE INKATIcs.oI Durmm Wommousa.—:On New Year's Eve all the inmates of Dut- ton workhouse were provided with a capital tea, by Mrs. Campbell. The lovers of the much abused weed were given a supply, and to each of those who have not con- tracted "the vile habit" of smoking, an orange was pre- sented. Several views of scenery in America were shown by the magic lantern which was under the superintendence of Mr. Robert Wilson, of Warrington, who delighted the audience with his excellent singing. MERSEY MISSION TO Smixarr.—RuNconur Bakwczr.— The annual tea meeting in connection with this useful mission took place at the Mission-room, Bottom Locks. The room was tastefully decorated with mottoes and evergreens, and a splendid Christmas tree, laden with presents for the Sunday scholars, was suspended from the rafters. The oyes of the little folks glistened with delight as they rested on the socks and stockings, the comforters and crossovers, the parasols and petticoats, the oranges and other„things that hung on its branches. If a tree is knowu by its fruits the young ones will have a very good opinion of that tree. The tea was a great success and the meeting afterwards proved a bumper, many people failing to get in the room. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Meadowcroft, the resident agent of the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Co., who continues to take a lively interest in the work ef the Mersey Missions to Seamen, and especially the Runcorn branch, whose worthy missionary, Mr. William Shaw, so well deserves the help of all in his endeavours to uplift the boat people who are continually passing through the town. The Chairman said the past year had been a very SatisfaCtOrY one in connection with the mission. It might not be out of place before proceeding with the entertainment which had to follow to give an outline of the work that had been done during the past 12 months. From the statistics handed to him, he found that the number of visits to fiats and boats had been 5,073 ; persons addressed, 8,672; meetints held, 105, at which the attendance had been over 6,000. The Sunday school meetings held had numbered 104, the attendance at which had been 8,041; open air meetings, 16, the average attendance at which had been 174; band of hope meetings, 46, attendance 2,931; mothers' sewing meetings, about 30, with an attendance of about 495. This was a very satisfactory summary of what had been done during the past year. The power to carry on such a comparatively exteneive work was, to a great extent, owing to the kind support given by friends to Mr. Shaw and the managers during the year. The Revs. W. Preston and J. J. Bryant made a few remarks expressive of their sympathy with the work which is unsectarian—a fact which does not seem to be full known in the town, judging from the list of ministers present at the meeting.—A lively and first-rate entertainment was afterwards given, in which Messrs. TEA PARTY AND SALE OF WORK AT SODA'S CROSS, WID- NES.—On Wednesday evening a tea party was held in Simm's Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel, Widnes. Tea was followed by a miscellaneous entertainment and a sale of fancy and useful articles'. RUNCORN ORCHESTRAL Socmy--The members of this socie- ty gave their first concert for the season in Bethesda Congre- gational school room, on Wednesday evening. The band con- sisted of twenty performers, including several well-known Widnes amateurs. Mr. Ainsworth acted as conductor, Mr. Charles Powell, as leader of the orchestra, and -Miss Jukes, as accompanist. The instrumentalists were Mr. Thorp, first violin; Mr. Earp, second violin; Mr. Powell, viola; and Mr. Simpson, violoncello.

- Ruxoons &moor, Boaan.—The last meeting of the I Board, as constituted during the last three years, was held 1 on Wednesday. Canon Barclay presided; and there were I also present—Messrs. John Simpson, Peter Briscoe, Richard Lea, James Pritchard, and F. Rigby. A letter was read from Mr. H. G. Bolam, dated the Ist December, stating that Major Orred would have no objection to sell the site in Albert-street for a Board school, at the rate of 7s. 61. per square yard. Another comananication from Mr. Bolam, dated the 20th ult., was read by the clerk, and was to the effect that the site in question contained about 1,35 l yards. The Chairman said it was out of the question to think th• Board could possibly pay 7e. 6d. per square yard.—Mr. Pritchard, amidst laughter, suggested that the taking of the initiative in this matter should be left with the new Board.—Mr. Simpson considered the price asked for the land too much.—Me. Briscoe said he had ineasured the site, which contained 4288 yards.—The Chairman: Mr. Bolam says his measnrement was not a proper one.—lt was resolved to deter tile consideration of the question until the first meeting of the new Board.— Agnes Gunning, late of the Liverpool Board schools, and Ellen Dukes, who at present attends the Board school, were appointed candidate monitor.—lt was agreed, after a little conversation' that the first meeting cif the new Board should , be held on the following Wednesday.—The rest of the pro- ceedings consisted of the Taming of votes of , thanks, and occupied considerable time. Mr. 1 Simpson proposed in eulogistic terms, a vote of thanks to the chairman for his conduct during the ' last three years. Whatever some of their friends might think of their proceedings outside, he believed they all had the satisfaction of feeling they had acted conscientiously, and tried to faithfully carry ortt the provisions of the Educe- tion Act. They had fully considered the interests of the ratepayers financially, and had not been wishful to provide school accommodation until it was really required. The speaker also dwelt upon the harmony which had character- ised their deliberations during the last three years.—The motion was seconded by Mr. 7Les.—Mr. Pritchard remarked that it had the hearty support of all the members: and it was passed unanimously.—ln acknowledging the vote, in warm terms, She Chairman spoke of the success and efficiency which the members had worked-together during their term of office. If their oven trumpeter-was dead, they must sound their own trumpet. (Laughter. He moved that a hearty vcte of thanks be given to Mr. Rigby, the Law Clerk, who had tilled his office during the Last three years with much ability.—Mr. Pritchard, in-seconding the motion, spoke of the business-like way in which the clerk always discharged his duties.—Mr. Rigby euitably acknowledged the resolution. —A similar compliment was then paid to the vice-chairman (Mr. Simpson), on the ,motion of Mr. Briscoe, seconded by Mr. Lea; after which the proceedings terminated. RUNOOZIP PARLTAXBNTAILY DEBITING SOL:au:Y.— After a short recess the House re-assembled on Tuesday evening. The Speaker ;(!r. T. Handley) took his seat at ' eight o'cledc, and there was a fair attendance on both sides. The strangers' gallery;pretented quite a lively appearance, showing that the interest in the debate on disestablishment has lost 'tome of its irrterest. A new member (Rev. G. T. Simpson) was introduced to the Speaker by the member for Nottingham (Mr. F. Lake), and took his seat as member for Newark amid the cheers of the Opposition. The debate on the motion for disestablishment was resumed by the mem- ber for Winchester (Mr. H. Hankinson, jun.) He made a successful attempt to prove that the Church of England had an existence beforethe .English nation Itself, and that with the exception of a short period was independent of the Pope of Rome. He spent too much time wading through numberless dates and historical matters prior to the Refor- mation, and left himself no time to deal with the more interesting affairs nearer our own day. His elocution was of no mean order, and being his first speech in the House took most of the members by surprise. He will be a front bench man in the next Conservative Government. The Vice-president of the Council on Education (Mr. F. J. Nor- man) followed in a neat speech, and supported the motion. There was a Radical ring about his speech befitting one who sits for the metropolis of the Midlands. He reminded the Opposition of the persecutions which Dissenters had received at the hands of the law in days gone by, reading the sentence of Sohn Bunyan, which was enough to curdle the blood in one's veins. He referred to the statement made by the member for Wind- sor that Dr. Osborn and other Wesleyan s were against dis- establishment, and said the doctor was almost alone in his episcopal leanings. The member for Walsall (Mr. S. Pope), said that before the debate took place he was ins nebulous state on the question. This was said with an artlessness simply charming, and smoothed the way for a few quiet digs at the Opposition and tithes. The Leader of the Oppo- sition (Mr. W. J. Shore) wound up the case against the motion in a speech, which for brilliancy, logic, and cultured humour, has seldom been equalled in the Howe, and never surpassed. The way in which he turned Macauley on the Home Secretary, who had made a strong point of a rather cumbrous copy of that writer's history of England, was smart to say the least. The same may be said of a couple of quotations from Mr. Gladstone, as they applied to an objec- tion raised at an early stage of the debate by the member for Birmingham, that some words of Mr. Gladstone in favour of a State Church which had been quoted, had been written nearly half a century ago. Mr. Shore thought that not only was the motion before the House inopportune, but in- expedient and unjust. The speech was listended to throughout with the deepest interest, and was concluded with a peroration couched in language most chaste. The Prime Minister (Mr. Wm. Handley) moved the adjourn- ment of the debate. He will, therefore, speak next week, and the member for Sandwich will reply, when the vote will be taken unless he asks leave to withdraw, which is thought likely. The House will then go into committee on the Ballot Bill. The Licensing Question will form the sub- ject of the next important debate. The House rose at ten o'clock.

C'LEYEE OAPTIIRE BY A WARRINGTON POLICE.-A clever captive of a thief has been affected by a member of the Warrington police force. Sergeant Berry was proceed- ing up Buttermarket-street, on Thursday week, he noticed a man of suspicious character with a good coat in his possess- ion. The sergeant accosted the man, and questioned him as to how he came into possession of the coat. The mak I replied that a shop keeper at Leigh had given it to him. Sergeant Berry however was not satisfied with the anew, r and took the man into custody, when he admitted having stolen the coat from a shop door at Leigh. The Leigh police wore communicated with, and one of their officers I came over to Warrington. The result was that the prisoner was removed to Leigh, where he was charged on Monday before Mr. Johnson one of the magistrates, with having stolen a top coat, value 19s. 9d. the property of Emmanuel Shuffleton, clothier of Leigh. Prisoner, who was a tramp named James Dacey, 26 years of age, was sent to prison 1 for two months, with hard labour.

TICE DEATH OF MR. JOSEPU HARTLEY, OF RUNCORN. , —On Sunday morning, the Rev. Canon Barclay preached the ffineral sermon of Mr. Hartley, at the Parish Church, Runcorn. There was a good congregation. The Canon took for his text Psalm ciii. 15, 16 (Prayer Book version), "The days of man are but as grass; for he flourisheth as a flower of the field. For as soon as the wind goeth over it, it is gone : and the place thereof shall know it no more. He spoke of the deceased in terms of eulogy, and remarked that he was. a genuine specimen—almost the last in this place—of an old-fashioned Churchnaan ; a Conservative alike in politics and religion; a warm admirer of the union of Church anfl State, and strongly opposed to any change in the mode of conducting Divine service, even though his good sense admitted that certain changes might be rendered necessary by "the diversities of times and men's manners." At the conclusion of the service Mr. Johnson, the organist, played the Dead March in Saul. INQUESTS IT WIDNES.—On Tnesday, several in- quests were held at Widnes, by Mr. C. E. Driffield, County Coroner. The first took place at the Angel Inn, on the body of Richard John, the child of John Mason, labourer, 15, Irwell-street, which died on the let inst., from scalds received ,on the 27th ult. The deceased was being nursed by its 4 grandmother, an old woman named Elizabeth Foley, when she observed that the kettle was in a dangerous position and attempted to put it right, on which some at the boiling water went upon the infant. It was taken to Dr. McLenaan, who attended it up to the date of its death. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."—The second inquest was held at the Simms Cross Hotel, on the body of Margaret ILyons, widow, aged 69, of 83, Travis-street, who died on the . ; 2nd inst. from injuries received by burns on the 27th Nov. ' , Deceased lived with her son at the above address, and on the date mentioned she appeared a little strange in her manner, ,on Lyons going nut, at about seven in the evening. Ile returned in about twenty-five minutes, and 'found deceased lying under the table, with her clothes on fire. Her left leg ' and both hips were found to be burned. Dr. Cooper attended her to the time of her death. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."—The third inquest was also held at the Simm's Cross Hotel, on the body of a child named Edward, the son of Francis Digman, aged 58, of 1 Oxford-street, who was found dead in bed en the 3rd inst. The little one was taken to bed on the night of the 2nd inst. ; by its 'nether, and appeared to be in good health,.but on the &lowing morning it was found with its hands clenched, and its body much discoloured. The jury returned a verdict 1 of "Fonna dead."

DROWNED TN A Tun AT ST. HELENS. —A. sad fate betel a man named Joseph Emblem, 60 years of age, who resided at 23, Watery-lane, Sutton, some time between Fri- day night and Saturday. morning, at No. 7 Pit, Ilayenhead Collieries. It appears deceased, who was a labourer, went to his work at six o'clock on Friday morning, and worked at the mortar mill. He worked all day, and said to some person that he was going to work all night. His wife saw him about seven in the evening and got his wages from him, leaving him tenpence. About two hours after she went to his place at work with his supper, but not finding him there she went to his cabin, where she fell asleep, and was found there on Saturday morning by William Fenny, who had occasion to go to the mortar mill. After searching a short time, Fenny found deceased in a water tub, one of his legs being visible, and in such a position as to lead one to the Iconclusion that he had fallen in. His wife does not appear [to know anything of deceased after taking his supper. The body was conveyed home.

PROCLAMATION OF LAND I-F.A01113 MEETING.—Mr. Fon- STER, in replying to Mr. O'Kelly, said that the meeting at Brookboro', county Fermanagh, had been proclaimed in accordance with sworn information that a counter-Orange demonstration was to take place, and therefore public peace was endangered.—Mr. O'KELLY said there never was the slightest intention to bold a counter-demonstration by Orangemen in the district.—Mr. WatroLs rose tei order. He asked Mr. Speaker if the lion. gentleman was entitled to address the House after the question had been answered.— The SPEAKER said the son. member had a right to address the House at that point if he desired, but the practice, if in- sisted on, would cause great inconvenience, and would require further consideration.—Mr. O'KErzy said the con- stitutional rights of Ireland were in question, and he insisted on speaking. He denied that there was any serious intention of holding a counter-Orange demonstration on the occasion of the meeting at Brookboro'. He moved the adjournment of the House.— Mr. Manna seconded the motion for adjournment.—Mr. SEXTON said the Government bad acted on the information sent by a small clique of local landlords.—Mr. GRAY com- plained of meetings of the Land League in other parts of Ireland being suppressed.—Mr. FonsrEtt justified the action of the Government, and said thert were fonr magistrates who gave information that led to the meeting being pro- claimed.—Mr. Dawsom and Dr. Coramurs condemned the Government for suppressing public meetings in Ireland by aid of bullet and buckshot—Mr. T. D. SuLuvate said all the endeavours of the Government would ha fruitless to- suppress expression of public opinion in Ireland.- -Mr. Lnane C.arz.lar and Mr. Jus-rIN MCCARTHY censured the executive for suppressing the Brookboro' meeting.—The SOLICITOR GENERAL defended the action of the local magis- trates.—Mr. T. P. O'CoYffon said the information sent to the Irish Government with recard to the meeting was a lie and a slander on the people of Ireland.—Mr. BYRNE saki the magistrates of Ireland could get a set of people to do any- thing they required, and it was by aid from this class that the meeting was suppressed. The people of Ireland did not want coercion or military police, they did not want law Cloud laughter); but they wanted justice.- -Mr. Gill, The O'Donogbue, and NlP:Finegan censured the Irish Government for suppressing legal meetings.--Mr. o:Saarontrassv said the Chief Secretary for Ireland had been misled as regarded the tneeting at Brookborough, and he advised him to act with greatet caution for the future.— Mr. J. MARY and Mr. ARTHUR O'Corma said, in the present instance, the Government had attempted to pnt down free speech in Ireland, but they bad signally failed. —The House divided—For adjournment 38, against 301. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 8, 1881.

THE food supply of the people has long been a sub- ject of vast concern to political economists. The great and rapid increase of the population has driven the English people to seek breadstuffs and meat sup- plies in markets beyond their own shores, owing to the insufficiency of home production. There was a time within the first half of the present century when the English people depended solely upon their own fields I for grain; and when foreign grain was only admitted into British ports under high tariffs, it is recorded that, on what is asserted to be very good authority, the stocks of grain stored did not often exceed thirteen days' consumption in each year. The abrogation of the Corn Laws and the introduction of Free Trade paved the way to a wonderful development of the traffic with other nations in articles of food, a develop-. meat that has proved advantageous, not only to our- selves, but to our friends abroad. Our dependence upon other countries to make up the deficiencies in the produce of our own fields has led foreign cultiva- tors to lay themselves out for keeping pace with the ever-increasing demands of British stomachs. Vast prairies, never before tilled by the hand of man, have been laid under tribute, and growers of grain abroad have, through the fertility of the soil they cultivate, and by the dheap facilities afforded fortransit, been able to good the English markets, and to com- pete with British farmers on their own ground, in the matter of grain supplies. The advantage of this to the masses is that they now have a much larger loaf for less money than they could possibly have obtained before Richard Cobden, John Bright, and other labourers for the repeal of the Corn Laws and the adoption of Free Trade principles, carried their agitation to a successful issue. What has been true I in respect of grain supplies has been equally true of our supplies of animal food. The wilds of America and the pastoral lands of our Australian and Canadian Colonies have contributed the latter ,class of food to an exteat that our grandfathers never dreamt of; but notwithstanding this large influx of foreign animal food the price of fresh meat is maintained at a height beyond the means of thousands of the poor. The con- tinued spread of foot and, mouth disease amongst home cattle has caused regulations of such a strict character to be enforced at our ports, in regard to the importation of live stock, as hamper foreign cattle breeders and importers, and consequently prevent an approoiable increase in the supply of animal food. It is true that cooked meats arrive in ship loads upon our coasts, and that large cargoes of comparatively fresh dead meat are brought across the Atlantic to swell the home stocks of this description of food. All this finds a ready market, at prices that are prohibitive to a large body of the people; and until an increased supply is ob- tained, either tinder present or different conditions, the high price of butchers' meat is not likely to be reduced. A. ";bad meat case," which the authorities at Exeter have been inquiring into, reveals an un- pleasant state of things. The exterior surface of some meat which had been seized was found, on examina- tion, to be decomposed, and consequently unfit for human food. A oertain part within, however, was still untainted, audit was stated in the course of the inquiry that the outside was usually cut off and sold to poor people at a reduced price, the poor being " glad " to obtain it. It is difficult to realise how anybody could be glad to become possessors of such offensive refuse, 'but that it finds a sale among people who cannot give the price demanded for wholesome meat is evident. The consumption of such putrid flesh must undoubtedly 'lead to the outbreak of dis- ease, and it is essential -that those who make an effort to sustain life on disease-producing garbage must be protected against themselves by the punishment of •those who, for gain, traffic in the refuse. The Exeter magistrates, however, do not seem to have realised to the full the enormity of the offence, for the owner of the garbage was set at liberty on paying a sovereign, in addition to the court fees. We have above made alksaion to the arrangements that exist for the supply of &ad meat in the face of the restrictions imposed I in reference to imported live stock. Some time ago the I steamahip Great Eastern was chartered by Sir Daniel Gooch and others for the purpose of transporting s scheme it killedwa s luring large cargoes of meat from Australia, by taking cattle, England. havingThi theme ic.,palivagerto boara, and the ass would have saaterially increased the stock of butchers' meat, and lowered the price correspondingly. It is now said that the project has been abandoned, and the money contributed returned to the subscribers, but that a new company is being formed to send the monstre steamship to La Plata on alike business.

As there are a great many intelligent Englishmen who would be puzzled to explain why Cetewayo's dominions were invaded by British soldiers, it is seaway to be wondered at that the unlettered, savage ex-ruler of Zululand should not yet have die- oovered the reason for the invasion. The royal pri- soner is still kept confined in Cape Town Castle, where he is shown to curiosity seekers. A Dr. Miller, of Bouthsea, has just published an account of a Tisit

div.head: ME Ma'MINE
div.p: ME Ma'MINE

he has paid on the fallen monarch in his castellated gaol: C`.:ctwayo is a personage of large build, and., 4nvr.etdly as he looks and is, he flatters himself he is o, pedestrian of no mean powers. He complimented I Dr. Miller upon being the first big Englishman he had nos, and he said to Colonel Hassard "none of theminyour army is like this man." Cetewayo has evidently sore humour in his composition. When Colonel Hassard observed that it was necessary to have slim and active men as soldiers, the ex-Zulu Monarch jokingly said, "You like men who can run away." He backed up this joke with a challenge to run, when he obtained his freedom,, a race with Dr. Miller, and averred that he could beat him. He had, he said, often walked fifty-seven miles in a day. Whatever impression Dr. Miller carried away as to the physical prowess of Cetewayo, he left him with the idea that he was a "poor specimen oi intellec- tuality." How leng the ex•Zula Monarcli is yet to remain a captive, nobody seems to have the slightest idea. Asked when he hoped to regain his liberty, Cetewayo pertinently remarked, " I cannot tell; I never knew what the English wanted, or I should not have been here."

Iris not within the range of human foresight to measure what engineering skill can yet achieve. The ingenuity of Mons. Lesseps has already mingled the waters of oceans over a sandy .wilderness and shortened the passage of ships from Western Evaope to the Indies. Whilst the brilliant and veteran Frenchman is now eagerly urging the undeztaking of another, grand scheme for removing isthmuses and submerging sandy wastes by the oeedn'a billows, in the interests of commercial Progress, we have dis- closed at home a plan, evolved from the inner con- sciousness of Mr. C. King, of London, for bringing Ireland and Scotland and the northern parts of England into more immediate communication by means of an isthmus. This he proposes should be constructed between the Mull of Cantyre, on the Scotch coast, and Tor Point, on the Irish coast. The distance between these places is about nineteen miles, and the author of this new scheme states that the water passage is 474 feet deep at mid. current, but much shallower towards either shore. Mr. King remarks that the elevated lands on both the Scotch and [lrish coasts at the points mentioned afford " faailitiee for gravitating the materials requisite to form the isthmus;" and he computes that the superficial extent of land required would be little more than a square mile, whilst the average depth and breadth would be about one hundred yards. Mr. King is snoguine that his plan would succeed, that there are no engineering difficulties that could not be surmounted, and that if the task be accom• plished the connection set up by an overland route would bring the peoples of the three kingdoms into closer bonds of friendship, and lead to an improved condition of the agricultural population of the Sister Isle. The scheme is no doubt capable of realisation, but whether the " game would be worth the candle" is a question which we are afraid Mr. King will never live to see solved by either the Government or a private company, one of which he suggests should practically recognise his plan.

Tux second session of the present Parliament was opened in Thursday, when he Queen's Speech was read by Com- mission. The speech was looked forward to with great interoet by all politicians, in the expectation that it would foreshadow the programme of the Government during the most important of the Parliamentary Sessions held in modern times. Foreign matters were given the first position in the speech, and the country is assured that Her Majesty's Government continue to be on the most friendly and har- monious footing with foreign powers. The success of the European Concert is declared in the asaeverance that the frontier question between Turkey and Montenegro has been settled; and the world is informed that the determination of the frontier question between Turkey and Greece has not been lost sight of, and is not likely to be, by the present Ministry. The prompt vindicationof the Queen's authority in the Transvaal the Cabinet wilt at once undertake; and the desire expressed for the restoration of peace in Basuto- land, by friendly action, will probably do much to tone down the hostile feelings by which the Basuto have been stirred into action. The military struggle in Afghanistan has, we are told, been brought to a close; and, though the bulk of the British force has been drawn back within the Indian frontier, a military contingent will remain at Cvdaloar until a responsible Government shall have been established by the Afghans. Coming to domestic questions we are given in the speech a piece of appreciative news. There has been, we are told, a gradual, though not a very rapid, improvement in the trade of the country, and tbe revenue is likely, in consequence, to be far more satisfactory than was anticipated at the commenoe- ment of the financial year. The bedy of the speech is most weighty and important. It deals exclusively with Trish subjects, which will undoubtedly command, during the session, the chief attention of legislators. The distress in that unhappy country has, we are informed, been greatly diminished by the realisation of an abundant harvest; but the social condition of the country has assumed such an alarming charaoter that the existing laws are found to be insufficient for the vindfhation of order, and for the protec- tion of life and property and personal liberty of action. Parliament will be asked to endow the Government with ad. ditional powers by the passing of coercive measures ; but in asking for extraordinary powers, for the exercise of which the Conservative party have long been clamouring, the Government recognise the existence of grievances that ought not to have a being, and promise work of legislative improvement, net only in Ireland, but in Great Britain also. , This legislative improvement is to take the shape of a further development of the Irish Land Act of 1870, and the estabish- ment of county Governments, founded upon representative principles, and framed with the double aim of confirming popular control over expenditure, and of -supplying a yet Imore serious want by extending the formation of habits of local self-government. The working of the Irish Land Act of 1870 receives in the speech a measure of eulogy, which is chilled, however, by he admission that, under the strain of recent and calamitous years, the protection which the Act supplied in contributing to the security and comparative well being of the occupiers of the soil, without diminishing the value or disturbing the foundations .of property, has not been found sufficient either in Ulster or the .other provinces. The Government pro- posals are to remove all obstacles arising out of limitations on the ownership of property, and to afford facilities for a larger portion of the people obtaining, by purchase, a permanent proprietary interest in the soil. Whether the Act of 1870 merits the panegyric contained in the speech is a moot point with politicians, and the admission in the speech of its insufficiency id recent years will strengthen the hands of disputants, who will watch eagerly for the full disclosure of the Government scheme for meeting the present needs of Ireland. Whether the promised emenda- tions of the Act will be fashioned on the lines of the Irish Land Commission and deal in a radical spirit with the whole questions involved, or they will be shaped to secure the approval, however reluctantly, of the House of Lords, who will fight late, early, and often before surrendering any of their privileges, time alone will prove. 'Nothing short of a thorough and effective measure will satisfy either the Irish people or the majority of English electors, regardless of any action the hereditary legisla- tors may be induced to take. 'the present is not a time for half measures; and we greatly mistake the character of the present Ministry if they permit the shadow of the House of Lords to influence the perfection of a measure of justice and conciliation to our Irish fellow subjects. The observance and respect for existing laws must of necessity be insisted upon, and the Government will receive the support of the Conservative members in the application of coercive mea- sures Co the sister kingdom, since they have agitated all along for the suppression of lawlessness by more rigorous means than the laws at present operative permit of. But whilst the Conservatives would suspend the Habeas Corpus ' Act and revive the Peace Preservation Act, they have no , other suggestions to offer for pacifying and comforting the people whose discontent and lawlessness are the outcome of grinding and exacting Acts that would disgrace the Statute Book of any civilised nation. The present Government, whilst it declares its fixed intention to enforce order, holds out the olive branch in the promise to redress the grievances under which the people at present groan. The promise of county boards upon representative principles—a scheme for which English counties have long prayed—will go far to allay Irish discontent; and their application to Irish counties is merely a forestalment of English counties. The Speech is not too full of promises of work sought to ' be achieved during the melon, though it admits that the

THat WARRINGTON BLUE COAT BRUT HERLY SOCIETY. We gather iron an interesthig paper in the Transactions eel the Lancashire and Cheshire Historic Society that the origin of the Warrington Blue Coat School was a very hum- ble eine. In the year 1665 Mr. John Allen, a native of Wargington, machirknown his intention of leaving a legaser for the purpose of apprenticing "five several poore boys to amnia useful handicraft trade." On the death of Mr. Allen is 1177, the legacy of £lBO was paid, and at a public meeting of tie inhabitants convened about this time, it was decided to Tease funds to be employed in the extension of this plan. w ,in the year 1711 that this charity was first consti- bated an educational one and Church principles made part of its daily teaching. For nearly 70 years the "Blew" boys were clothed and educated only; butte 1775 it was purposed to add board and continuous supervision. To effect this desirable object a large ieutlay was necessary. A special subsoriotien was entered into, headed by John Blackburne, Imo., with £5OO, and the present school house was built. The school was trued in 1782, and to celebrate the event Mr. Owen, the then Rector of Warrington,preached a special sermon at the Parish Church entitled, "The resources of Ciaristian charity," which was published. We extract the following note:—" 1 is a fact which ought not to be con- sealed (because it tends to benefit the charity by a dis- tinguished example), that Dr. Enfield, though a minister, in tie separation honoured these sentiments by an expressive stark of his approbation, a liberal contribution, in which he has been followed by several members of his society." In 1555 on the recommendation of the charity commissioners the day school was discontinued and the work of the institu- tion confined to the maintenance, education, and training of the children elected on the foundation. He defied them to show him anybody who had a greater amount of influence over the people than the Roman Catholic priests in Ireland; and upon the way in which they discharged their duties would depend to a very great extent the state of affairs in Ireland. Having allqded to the bravery of the English soldiers he pointed out that the restraint which they practised in Ireland when they were insulted and spat upon was very praiseworthy, seeing that not a single ease could be quoted in which the men under command had for- gotten themselves. They had heard from General Roberts how well the English army had marched and fought under trying difficulties, and they had every reason to be highly gratified with the army. Although they had not seen so much of the navy, yet they had lately seen how the marines could help the army at the Cape when they were called upon. The auxiliary forces had done a great deal of good in doing away with alarms for they were quite pre- Pared to defend the country against invasion by any foreign power. They bad a force something like 200,000 that could be called out at once to defend their homes and their country, and he was of op'nion that the auxiliary forces could easily be augmented to about 400,000 or 500,000 men if it was needed. Mr. Bretcaeee proposed "The Mayor and Corporation of Warrington," and in doing so said he was old enough to remember the time when the town had no Corporation, whereas now on all sides they saw manifestations of the great imprevement that had been made in the local govern- ment of the town of Warrington. In the old days there was ta kind of annual festival at the selection of the Borough Reeve, when a visit was paid to the lord of the manor, but a sort of listlessness and inactivity was prevalent without any kind of sanitary improvement being made. There was a good deal of rollicking and rougle joking as he understood that one of his ancestors at one time assisted in pulling up part of Bridge-street. (Laughter.) That was in the days when the old watchman went about singing "A fine morn- ing, past 5 o'clock,"—(renewed laoghter)—and so Warring- ton went on without any improvements whatever being made. But when the mayor and corporation was established, then the town commenced to improve. He remembered taking part in the walking. of the boundary for the first time, for the Blue Coat School band was called out, and be (the speaker) as a sort of dignitary in that band had to take part. (Laughter.) The improvements that had taken place year by year since then showed that there was a great deal of what the Americans mould call "go-a-headism " in the town, and he looked forward to the time when they would have the electric light in their streets and establishments, when Warrington would brae port and that wonderful canal had been made, when Warrington would be independent of Liverpool, the latter having retired on-a pension from its dock (lees. (Laughter.) He hoped that Warrington would make as rapid strides in the future as in the past, and he asked them to drink "Success to the Mayor and Corporation of Warrington," coupling with he .toast the name of Coun- cillor Edward Greenall. He was 'quite satisfied that NVarringten had made more rapid strides during the last ten years than it had ever done done in its history pre- viously. They had bad many important acceseions during those years, such for instance as the Tpivn Hall and park, the purehase of the gas works, the improvements of the strcets, and last but not least the very important sanitary improvements which he thought justified his statement that more improvements had been effected during the last ten years than during the previous history of the population. He also stated that the rate of mortality had decreased during the last few years, and he hoped that eventually all the ratepayers and the town would benefit by the improvements that had been made. The rules of the Blue Coat Bretherly Society spoke in the highest terms of the education which the children received in the school, whilst the scripturalr instruction given lay upon them burdens throughout lifec and their conduct in after life proved that they were worthr recipients of those blessings. He amazed at the statements made, from which iwouldár %Mat Churchmen 200 years ago were a set of scoundrels, and the Conservatives were little better. All the suffering of Ireland had been laid at their door by Mr. Bright, and he I urged that past history and the facts recorded should be studied so that their young men might be able to hold their own, no matter what was said on the other side. He feared that he had exceeded the bounds of what was usual on that occasion—(hoar, hear,)—but be could not help addressing tke young men present. When .boys at 14 years of age left school and were thrown upon their own resources without any means of sup- port therilhe society stepped in and helped them if they showed any anxiety to conduct themselves properly. (Ap- plause.) He thought the money subscribed by the various gectlemen could not be applied to a better purpose. (Ap- plause.) He drew the attention of those present to the clause in the report which said that "the committee again repeat tbatgreat encouragement would be afforded them by a more general co-operation of those who are indebted for their education and training either as day scholars or Blues to the institution, and who as yet have not become members of the society. If all old scholars rallied round the society and became members the funds would be increased, the com- mittee stimulated in their exertions, and the sphere of the society's usefulness largely extended." He asked all the Old scholars present who were not members to become so. He then proposed the health of Dr. Bowes, the founder of the loCiety, coupled with that of Alderman Joseph Davies who had helped very much in promoting the establishment of the society. The toast was drunk with musical honours, after which Dr. Bowns said he thanked them very much for that re- newal of their kindness to him. It was the business of his life to do all be could for the benefit of the Blue Coat School. and he took a very great interest in his work. (Ap- plause.) Alderman J. DAVIES, also responded, stating that Dr. Bowes had been the first to move in the work and that he had simply helped him to carry it out. Mr. Birchall had said that they had come from a chrysalis state to a beautiful butterfly. (Laughter.) Well he would take them back to the chrysalis state. An old lady recently told him that she had seen the mayor go to church with thirty-two policemen to take care of him. She declared that she had never before seen such an extravagant expenditure of public money in blue cloth and bright buttons, for she remembered the time when the town was governed by one man—Paul Caldwell— and he did it very well, for when he saw two men fighting he let them fight it out. (Laughter). He proposed as the next toast the "Kindred societies" with which he coupled the name of Mr. Houghton. (Applause.) They were all en- gaged in the same good work, and he had no doubt the Blue Coat society of Liverpool was doing all it could in the same direction. - • _ Dr. BOWES said that the idea of establishing the society was not an original one, as he obtained it from Liverpool, and he therefore regarded the Liverpool society as the parent of their's. (Hear, bear.) - • '- Mr. HOUGHTON, in acknowledging the. toast, said that as the head master of the Blue Coat Hospital, he had not many opportunities otvisiting, but itr was quite a pleasure to come and Bee their first offspring of the Bluq -Coat school at Liver- pool. As to the work of these societies, he thought no one but those who had experience of them could tell the immense advahtages that accrued therefrom. It was not merely a question of pounds shillings and pence assistance, but there were many lads who wanted counsel ,and advice when they went out into the world, and it Wu then that a brotherly word Of advice was felt to be needed. At such a time many a lad whose career was a bright one had been saved by being taken in hand by one in whom he had confidence, and in rendering such aid these societies did much for humanity. (Applause.) There was a similar institution at Oldham, but it was more of a benevolent society than a brotherly, and also at Chester a like institu- tron had been established. In Liverpool their society did not help the sisters as they did at Warrington, but a separate institution, managed by ladies, did so. (Applause.) Councillor Scrnars proposed "the health of the-Chair- man," of whom he spoke in eulogistic terms, and' the•toast ITU drunk with irusical honours.

ALLSGBD EMBEZZLEMENT.—Erwin Flynn, a private of Her Majesty's 22nd Regiment, stationed at Newry barracks, Ireland, was charged, as a servant, with having embezzled £8 Sc., the property of the trustees of the London and North- Western Railway Locomotive Insurance Company, on the 15th Sept.—The prisoner was remanded until Friday.
BUTTERMARK ET-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, WARRINGTON.

The annual tea party in connection with this seaool was held on Monday evening. About 150 persons partook of tea, which was served in the lower room, the followiug ladies presiding over the trays :—Mrs. Gornall, Mrs. Carter, Mrs. John Taylor, Mrs. Henshall, Mre. TOft,Mrs. Gleave, Mrs. Collin, Mrs. Sanderson, Mrs. Bailey, and Mrs. Dutton. After tea an adjournment was made upstairs, where a public meet- ing was held, presided over by the ,ReV. E. 0. Coleman. There was a good attendance. During the evening songs and duets were sung by the scholars, Mr. J. Muir officiating at the piano. Miss Richardson and Miss Robinson sang a duet entitled, "Go on, thou shining river;" Miss Houlds- worth and Mr. Silcock, "When the wind blows from the sea;" and Miss Richardson, "The mill wheel." The Secretary's report, read by Mr. Henshall, commented on the fact that the year just closed was the centenary of Sunday schools. Among all the wondrous changes and revolutions which the past century had witnessed was there one more glorious or that had exerted a mightier influence on the world than Sunday schools, which, though only commenced a hundred years ago by Robert Raikea, of, honoured memory, had spread with such rapidity that they had long been recognised as a great national institution, and which occupied the warmest place in the affections and regard of all sects and denominations of Christian people? Their Methodist forefathers in Warrington were among the earliest to catch the holy infection ; for it was found that the school whose interests they were met to promote that night was founded in 1786, only six years after Raikes opened his school in Gloucester • and who could say bow many had been brought to a knowledge of the truth through the instrumentality of that institution, thug being prppared for a life of usefulness? It would be seen that the centenary of this school would soon arrive, and the committee offered no apolo2y for again earnestly pressing upon the Wesleyans of the Warrington circuit the urgent necessity that existed for providing better and more commodious accommodation for the development of the school than the present incon- venient and obsolete structure afforded. (Applause.) The church had long recognised the meat importance and value of Sunday schools-as the chief source from which it must look to have its ranks recruited. The importance attached to the training of the young by the other denominations in Warrington was evinced by the commodious and cenVenient structures they had provided; and they (the Methodists) must feel when they compared with those their own dingy, shabby, and altogether inadequate building, that the time had come when this long-standing reproach, to them as Methodists should be wiped out by a hearty and united effort. (hear, hear, and applause.) The committee 'earnestly hoped that this question would be taken up, so that they might be able to celebrate the centenary of their ~Sunday school in very different premises from the present. In spite of the difficulties with which they had been sur- rounded during the past twelve months their labours had been owned and blessed by God in a very striking manner. In his report for 1879,.the secretary (Mr. Ford) referred to the year's work in these terms :—"The year just ended presents no striking features nor extraordinary success." They were glad to be able to make a very different report to that for 1880. The results of many years of patient work had suddenly been made manifest, amt 'upwards of 60 of the scholars had made a full consecration, of their hearts and lives to their Saviour. (Applause.) They would all join in the prayer that the Lord would establish and strengthen them in every good work, that they might grow in graced ind in the knowledge and love of our Lord and Onoriout Jesus Christ. The number of scholars on the Looks aVer.age attendance for the year showed a very satis- factory increase over last year. The number on the books vas:—Boys 212, girls 187, total 399, being an increase of 61. The average attendance was—morning 128, afternoon 268, against 98 morning, 230 afternoon, for 1879. The num- ber of teachers and officers was 42. The committee would I avail themselves of this opportunity to testify their cordial appreciation of their services.a. The librarian, Mr. W. Parkinson, reported that the library had been used by about 80 scillblars, which was as many as the books would accom- modate. The Band of Hope, which fcr some little time had been inactive, had been re-established; and, under the management of Mr. Prince, as secretary, gave promise of great success, having already 36 members. After referring to the resignation of Mr. Ideate* is Imperintendent of the school, the report stated that time. 'Juvenile . Missionary Society had done good work during the past year, and would be able to pay over to the parent society about PA. A collection had also been made in the school for the Chil- dren's Home in London which realised £2 7s. 6(1. In con- clusion, the committee felt that tha gracious movement now going on in the school would entail upon the managers , heavy responsibilities, and they would ask for the sympathy and prayers of those present, and that God would encourage and cheer His servants, the teachers, in their work. (Applause.) The CnatitmArr then called upon Mr. CARTER to read the treasurer's report. The total in- come of the school had been £4O 108., £4O of whifh had ' been the result of the anniversary collection. The expendi- ture had been £5l 3s. 6d. There was also £l4 lie. Id. due to the treasurer, which made the total debt of £2:5 4s. 7d. About three years ago the freehold of the school and the land and two houses adjoining were purchased, and the debt then amounted to about a thousand pounds. Since then there had been £4OO paid off, and there was now only £6OO owing, and he hoped they would be able in a few years to go hi for a new school. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN having paid a compliment to the secre- tary for his excellent report, Mr. Isaac, superintendent of the school, said the end and aim of Sunday school teaching was the conversion of chil- dren, but many people expressed doubts as to whether that could be. If that doubt could be removed it would be a great step in advance. There was great improvement in the order of the school, but the accommodation was very defi- cient. When children were converted many thought they shonld be staid and quiet, but it wasalot so. On the con- trary, the giving te God of life and love made them juyous sad happy, and he hoped that parents would not think that the children were bad if they were rather frolicsome. (Hear, hear, and applause.) • Mr. Lamplugh, circuit minister, Mr. Stringer, of Widnes, aid Mr. Ford then addressed the meeting on the desirability of building a new school. Rev. W. Baia-rim:rutty spoke on the evils against which Sunday school workers had to contend. There was a dan- gerous spirit of sFepticistn and unbelief prevalent arpor,ig the people of the day. ,I was a scepticism whicb,regarded-the great Redeemer as a moral tea Cher before his time, it looked down upon Christianity as a system out of date, and con- sidered mere morality as the sure way to happiness and safety, whilst creeds and catechisms were priescraft. Young people were in danger from this spirit, and they must be taught so as to stand out for the truth, and shown that by holding to the falacies of unbelief they had nothing to gain but everything to lose. Another danger arose from the rage for questionable and sinful amusements. That such a danger existed VMS testified to by the advertising columns in die newspapers, and by the sorrowful experience of , thousands who had given promise of piety, but who were 'now lovess of pleasure and not ef God. Amusements that were innocent were necessary, and ought to be enjoyed. The attendance at theatres, ballrooms, and dancing saloons might be considered a very little thing, but it was often the way to •destruction. (Applause.) Young people must be guarded from these amusements. The drinking customs of the country were another great source of 'danger, and could only be controverted by inculcating the principles of total abstinence. (Applause.) Many ministers of religion were total abstainers, and in Richmond College, out of 70 students, there were 68 teetotallers. (Applause.) These were some of the dangers to which young people were subject; let them endeavour to save them by means of the pulpit, of Sabbath schbols, of mutual improvement classes and bands of hope, and they would exert such an influence for good as would bear fruit after many days. (Applause.) Mr. NICHOLSON, Mr. WEAVER, and the Rev. J. A. Mawr then spoke on Sunday school work, urging the necessity for in- creased accommodation.

PENKETIT :WORKMEN'S CLUB. OPENING OF NEW PREMISES. :The members of thlePenketh Workmen's Club have recently removed to new premises erected by Mr. James Turner, and on new year's flay the building was opened. The premises are more commodious than those formerly occupied by the club, and consist of reading, billiard, and smoke-rooms, on the ground floor, a capital concert or lecture room being above. Besides being more adapted to meet the require- ments of the members than the old club rooms, the new building possesses the additional advantage of being of con- siderably lower rental, an item of great importance to a club which cannot boast of a large number of members. The billiard room was nicely decorated with evergreens, dm., and mottoes were placed about the rooms setting forth the evil results of idleness and intemperance. The opening cere- mony took place in the large room shortly after seven o'clock, when there was a fair attendance. The chair was occupied by Councillor Monks, and amongst those present were Messrs. R. Garnett, D. Garnett, J. Turner, W. Wheeler, Pickton, T. Garnett, J. Mainley,

, - The Crummier, after wishing the meeting a happy and 1 prosperous new year, said he had come to talk to them and express a few ideas in connection with the object for which they were met that night. He was told that the primary ' object of the club was to provide a sort of home for the 1 young men of Penketh. That in itself was a very desirable thing. He thought they might make a .mistake sometimes 1 by not making that provision for young people which they I required ; and; it very frequently happened that if they I did not provide a healthy source of amusement the young people would provide themselves with an unhealthy source of amusement. (Hear, hear.) Therefore he thought it was a very proper thing to establish in the centre of a village like that, a room in which they could meet together, and where they could endeavour to cultivate their intellectual and moral faculties, and at the same time not overlooking the physical, because a healthy mind required a healthy body. Speaking from his own experience, he said they would have two clasillsof persons who would probably take advantage of the iniritution. There would be thoee who would take advantage of it in order that they might use the facilities which it offered to promote their own intellectual growth and development, and there would be those who would take advantage of it as a 4/leans of pleasure, and as a rule that class of people did not look beyond the present time. He wished to impress upon all young men who were entering on what be should call life, a desire to be something more than the average of men. They were very frequently inclined to look at men in higher positions than themselves, and think if they had similar advantages how much they could do. Bat he had lived long enough to find out that to a very large extent men made their own posi- tions. Hedid not mean to say that every man could become a Gladstone or a Beaconsfield, but he did say that in this country there was a very wide field for any man who was endowed with something more than average ability, and that by making use of the opportunities thrown in their Way they could turn them to their own advantage and to thy advantage of those about them. (Hear, hear.) It rested very much with the men themselves. He had known several young men in his time—he was now going back 'sonic 30 years—who took advantage otthe Warrington Mecharlics'ilnstitute, which was an institution of the same character as they were seeking to establish at Penketh, and in the face of alm2st every disadvantage youths could start with, by force of dharacter, dogged perseverance, and self- reliance, they raised themselves to positions of respectability and eminence, and of great usefulness. But it was not done by preferring the present at the expen.se of the future. As there was no royal road to wealth there was no royal road to improvement except by downright bard work, hard study, and self-denial. If the young men of Penketh were disposed to set about it in earnest to improve themselves, he bad not a shadow of doubt in his mind that at any rate if they did not become the Gasnett's of Penketh they would be all the better for the efforts they had put forth. There was another thing which he was quite sure would result from such efforts. Speaking within his own experience, he did not hesitate to say he had had more opportunities of giving what the world called a "good lift" to young men than he had found young men qualified for the good lift which he was disposed to give them. (Hear, hear.) He thought that was the experience of men who had had the management-of large businesses. It was a melancholy thing to see so many young men growing up who did not seem to have a thought beyond the mere sensual pleasures of the day, who had not a- thought of the future, and as to what was to become of them when they got middle-aged or old men. (Applause.) But the class of young men who had made it their business to,think and develope the faculties that God had given them they found somehow or other, by degrees raising themselves above the average of their fellows. There was one great trial which young men wh! might be struggling in their condition of lifenow had to undergo, in respect of which he would give them a word of encouragement. They would meet with a good deal of tyranny and a good deal of jealousy from fellow-workmen, but such young men he would encourage to perse7ere. They would outlive the opposition, and the man who had done as much as he possibly could to injure him would, years after, be the very man to encourage him perhaps the most. One was. fficiinel to think Penketh was developi much more rapidly and much more promieiiigT than that meeting indicated, but while they might be few in number majorities were not by any means the test of great success' If he were a young man of Penketh he would endeavour to .rintite the institution a success byshis own indLeidual effssets_ He would rely no more upon Messrs. Garnett thanAessnould possibly help. (Hear, hear.) He knew Messrs. garnett would be glad at any time they could, bat' he noticed that however willing men might be disposed to help others they liked to see others make some effort to support‘ themselves and do the best they could for themselves. 40 far as Warrington was concerned, he was rather ashamed to say that there seemed to be a feeling that everything should be done for working- men but they should do nothing for themselves. Wherever that feeling got to be uppermost they might rest satisfied it would destroy all the independence and all the pleasure that was to be derived by establishing clubs like that. He would seek to make the club independent, and if the mem- bers found at the year's end they were in debt after each man felt he had contributed all he could with due regard to the wants of his family, he did not think there would be any difficulty in making up the difference that might be re- quired. He counselled them to sae to the prompt collec- tion of subscriptions, and urged each member to consider it a matter of business to pay his subscription in time, re- marking that sound financing in clubs like theirs was just as necessary as sound financing in business. (Hear, hear.) If they did so he was pretty well satisfied, that they. might be able,,to establish the elub with satisfaction to themselves, and so long as they were out of debt they would find plea- sure in ',going there. He thought in all matters it was very desirable they should cultivate a feeling of toleration towards one another—(hear, hear)—and hoped if ever they were tempted to depart from this line they :would.bring themselves to reflect that every man had aa,much right to his opinions and convictions as they had 'themselves. If they did that he was satisfied both 'Conservatives and Liberals might work harmoniously together, and tend to promote the common good qf Penketh. In conclusion, he stated that if there was-. a young man in connection with that institution who soug.,bt self improvement and practised that self denial which Was so necessary especially in Eng- latini, he 'was sure that young man would not want for Mends; and he thought he would not want for other assistance if at any time he should need it • and if they qualified themselves for the effort which would be required he was satisfied the effort would be well repaid. (Applause.) Mr. JAMES Tunsenn hoped the Workmen's Club would be a success. He thought he had shown sufficient interest irl preparing the conveniences for it.to be silch,(applatiee)— and he hoped they would do their part to make it a success. (APPlease.) , s sr ' • - • • Mr. Beyne_gatesenTT said be thought the club was not by any means exclusidely for young men. Although he was very ftruch'iriterestecl in the young men Of Penketh it was well understood that married men, and those who were getting grey hairs, were welcome. The club was for those 'of all ages, all creeds, and all politics, but embraced only those who conducted themselves becomingly, and conformed to the rules of the institution. It was 18 .years since a shinier institution was foutided in Penketh. It was a sort of mechanics' institute, big after two or tliiale years it died like many .others from lac of, support. They met together about four years.ago and embodying the same rules started the present club. The old instituthan left a balance in the bank, and although that cotild not be said of them, he be- lieved if all their debta were paid they would not be a penny in debt. (Applause.) He thought that was some- thing for them to congratulate themselves upon, . (Ap- plause.) Mr. ROBERT GARNETT congratulated the members of the club on having secured such good premise's. They seemed to be all that a dab could desire, and they had the addi- tional advantage of not being in connection with a publih tap. Referring to the remark ref the ,Chairman, that,there were many persons whoawirjd ba glad to giyes striving people a lift if they had the right stuff in them, he saisl if that club was to degenerate intO a place' in 'winch young men played cards, draughts, or billiard S; ti the d'febision ilf other things, his feeling would be that it was a mistake it was ever owned. There were higher purposes in life. Men were created -for higher., and nobler purposes than to fritter away the time God had given them in things which tended to demoralise them and perhaps to bring thenwlown to that which was brutish. If anything pained him it was to see young men xeitla a want of ambition. . Young men should strive to be better men than their fathers. They had better opportunities for acquiring knowledge and there were other advantages in the reach of young men which he was sorry they did not avail themselies Of. What thby shoeld aim at was to improve-the times iii'which ehti tivid. x The man who was capable of .elevtition' elevated himself. pltdid not Matter what position he was .ig,lse, goit2 thestop. What he would like to see was the ..,yoiing men pf .Penketh, striving, to raise themselves sociallyi morally,. and intellectually, and to make themselves bteter iiiereiliertl-of "society, and More useful in the Nyolid. Thereswasenot a batten iiiuStration of what a man might he than tould be' found in their Chair- man. (Applause.) • SArnanev.—Before Alderman Burgess. THREATENING WITNESSES —John Carr was charged with threatening Harriet Chriines, Mary Brett, and Ann McCarty, orrthe Previous day. The complainants had given evidence agairst the prisoner on a charge of felony, but on the prisoner being discharged when leaving court, he threatened to kick the t omplainants. He was ordered to find two sureties of £lO to keep the peace for six months in default to go to gaol for 14 days. MONDAY.—Befo-e the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) Major Cartwright, and Councillor Crosfield. Patrick Roach was charged with being drunk in Butter- market-street, on Saturday, and was fined ss. and costs.— John Conway for a similar offence at Market Gate on Satur- day, was fined ss. and costs.-4 Catherine Melior was fined ss. and costs, total 16s. 6d., for being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, on the 27th ult., and assaulted Mrs. Ann Holland, of the Brittania public-house.—Mary Ann Quinn was ordered to pay the costs for being drunk and disorderly in Dolman's-lane, on the 27th ult.— Mary MalloneY for being guilty of a like offence in Buttermarket-street, on the 27th ult., was ordered to pay costs.—James Oxworth had the costs 3s. 6d. to pay for being drunk and disorderly at Market Gate, on the 24th ult. • STREET OmyrancnoN.—ThomasWhitlow was summoned for obstructing Bridge-street, on the 24th ult., by allowing a horse and cart to stand there an unreasonable time. P.C. Monaghan proved the case, and the defendant was fined 2s. ed. and costs. A WIFE BEATER BENT TO PRlSON—George Pritchard was charged with assaulting his wife on the previous Friday.—The complainant said her husband came home drunk and assaulted her, afterwards knocking the furniture about..—The prisoner pleaded guilty and was sent to gaol for a month. FRAHM:MEM ErrusugErr. James Rowlands was charged with having fraudulently enlisted in the 14th Brigade by declaring himself to be a bachelor when he was a married man.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, saying he was orry ; he could not get work.—Provost Sergeant Cambridge ski the prisoner's character was good, these cases, however, were getting very numerous. The prisoner who had ren- dered himself liable to three months imprisonment, wap sent to prison for one month's hard labour. ' • I, A PUBLICAN SHUMONED FOR ALLowneo DoatneozPnevpro. mi. Alfred Tanks, occupier of the Bear's Paw, Buttermarket- alleet, was summoned for having, on the 27th ult., allowed, dominoe playing for money, to be carried on in his pretniaes.' —Mr. Graham appeared for the defendant, and pleaded not gfillty.—...lnspector Profit said about 7-15 od Monday night, the 27th ult., he in company with P.S. Berry, visited the Bear's Paw public-house. In the back room Mg,' saw four men playing dominoes. They had to pass through Oat room to tile parlour. He said to the defendant "If !fere you 1 Sholld stop that game." He said: "Pp, they are doing-no-him." Witness said: They are doing hermit they are playing for money or money's worth. Defendant said "Well, they are only playing for their own drinks." Witness replied "That is gaming; it is illegal."—Major Cartwright : Were they unruly.—lnspector Proffit : Oh no, sil.—Major Cartwright: Quite sober? Inspector Proffit : Yes, Sir.—Cross examined by Mr. Graham: Witness said when he came to Warrington there was a good deal of dominoe playing. But they had instructions from the Chief Constable to put a stop to it, and they did so to a great extent; but now the practice wis beginning again.—He did not see any money pass; and did not hear anyone say they were playing for money's worth except defendant. He did know that there was a notice up in the house prohibiting gaming.—Major Cartwright (to defendant): How long have ,ou kept the house? Defendant: Seven months.—Councillor Drosfield ; Have you ever been warned by Mr. Hunt about this. Defendant: Never.—Major Cartwright 'r We have no -edtiveproOf before us to-day, that these men were playing ,Irink.—Major Cartwright: I want to fusk is it lawful for tnife'playilominoes at all? The Clerk: Oh, yes. /he Ich, however, decided to hear defendant's witnesses. Jefenclant was then sworn, and he said be had occupied the house since May last. The men were neither playing for 'alley nor money's worth. When the inspector came he" asked if dominee playing was illegal, but did not say the 'then were playing for glasses of drink. The men did not complete the game.—By Councillor Crosfield The had never playeclfor "glasses round" in his house. Alexander Mi4kieplabourer, said he was playing dominoes when the inspector came in. He denied that they played for money or money's worth. They played for love. Thomas Argyle Ward give similar evidence, and the .bench dismissed the case.—The Mayor did not sit during the hearing of this case. • , LICENSE TR&NSPHRS.—The following transfers of licenses were granted ;—The Lower Angel, from John Craddock to William HumPhries ; Millstone Inn, from Thomas Hodson Farnworth" to John Gamble, Stevenson; Vine Tavern, from Charles Holland to John Craddock ; The Three Pigeons, from William -Marshall to TOM Orlando Phillips; The Smiths' Arms, Legh-street,'"from John Mather to Joshua McElroy; premiss in Mersey-street, from Jane Tooth to David Smith •, premises 60. MEETINS AT ST. HELENS.

MR. PICKARD AND THE MINERS. A Well attended meeting of, niiners was held On the Fair Ground, St. Helens; on Saturday afternoon, Mr. Thomas Glover, check-weighman at the Haifa& collieries, presiding. There were also on the raised platform Mr. John Cross, who has been working energetically during the last few months on behalf of the miners, and who has succeeded in a measure in bringing together the scattered forces and uniting them for the purpose of defending their interests, and Mr. McKay, and Mr. Woods. Daring the proceedings a drizzling rain fell which made standing very unpleasant, but the audience listened attentively to the speakers. The Clutzucts said they were met together to eonsider the wages question, the best means of securing better or- ganieation, and also to speak upon the the Employer's Liabi- lity Bill. They were J.II very important subjects, and i ought to be considered n a proper spirit. They all wanted better wages, but in order to secure that they must have bet- ter organisation, for it was by organisation they were enabled to uphold themselvesrand keep the masters from trampling upon them as they had done in the past. As to the Em- ployers Liability Act other gentlemen would speak on that. He would ;therefore call upon Mr. Cross to address " them.

• Mr. %Ross laid they would be very' glal to get more wages, bat the masters said they could not give them more. He had sh3wn however, to them:at their meetings and through tle public press that masters could afford to give them more wages. The masters said that the price of coals ,wp so low 'that they could not really advance the wages. But what were the facts: in 1877, the price of coals was es. id. and to day it was es. 2d., and he thought that was a very good advance in the profits of the Madera, and they "(the colliers) had a very good case to show that they were not asking anything unreasonable from their masters. (Hear, hear.) But the masters would say " Ah, but we don't get 91. 2d. on all the „coals we raise; we have contracts, and these contracts are made at such low rates that it really does not run us more than 2d. or 3d. a ton." But the col- hers, were not responsible for:that, and labour and capital ought to be so bound together, and work so laarmonitisly that when trade was brisk the colliers should have a proportionate share in the profits, as they were pushed when trade was bad. The time had now arrived when they ought to have their wages advanced at the very least 15 per cent. and on-Mon- day they contemplated asking the masters for that advance, and he hoped the masters would accede to their re- quest, and thus obviate the necessity of resorting to a strike or lock-out. They deserved the advance, as they had been working five years at almost starvation point. The colliers had been suffering as no other Englishman would suffer, and they stood worse at the present day than at any period since the commencement of the coal trade., They were actually working for 18s. a week! (Shame.) Forty-five years ago they were winding 1,000 tons of ooal, but now they were using over 10,000 tons per day, and they were increasing every year, consequently they had to go deeper, and they suffered more from bad ventilation. (Hear. 'hear.). They would never improve unless they organised, and the masters could reduce their wages one by one and the colliers could not resent that interference. He had been to a lawyer's office about a case that very morning. The men had been stopped because they could not get certain wages. They left work, and when they demanded their wages the mister said they had left without notice and must have no wages. (Shame.) As soon as the men had got out of the pit others were put in their places. If they had beetf organised that would not have occurred, the men would., not, have taken their places as was the ease at present (A Voice:' "There is one standing beside you.") Mr. Cross said that he had been doing his beet by posting bills throughout the district, and the masters had sent after him men who pulled them down again. Referring tO the Employers' Liability'Bill; he said the masters were afraid of that bill, and endeavoured tck contract themselves out of it. The bill was as simple as A B C, and the men eotild get no compensation unless it could he proved that accidents were the result of the masters negligence. A good proportion of accidents was traceable to the fault of the masters, and consequently (and naturally too) they were afraid of the bill, which had been passed on behalf of the workmen. They had at the present day a good many managers who held certificates but were net prac- Aical men' and in many cues they only knew the condition of the pit from the report of the fireman. It was quite ob- vious that the bill had been passed in order, to more effec- tually secure the safety of the men, and he itetvised them not to al'grt.tee papers which the masters laid before th'em to the'effect that the men would not abide by the'Act,.for it 'would be suicidal to do so, and they:would be doings most wicked action. „ Mr. Mcifav next addressed the meeting, and spoke chiefly on the Employers' Liability let. He observed that the em- ployers were saying that 15 per cent, of accidents in the pit vere,uot.the fault of the master, so that any compensation the men could recover would be very small indeed. But he said the reports of juries showed that a great propor- tion of the accidents irhich took place from 1849 to 1879 had been traced to the neglect of the employer or his manager, for whose act the master was responsible. He gave several instances Flaring out this statement, and in many cases claimants ha obtained compensation under the Mines Regulation Act.

Mr. Jonw WOODS. of Ashton, addressed the meeting, and showed that in order tp get an advance of wages men must unite themselves in one great whole. Neal. the 'close of the meeting a little disturbance traa caused by one person who objected to a resolution proposed by Mr. McKay, to the effect that those masters who had been trying te contract themselves out of the Act should be censured and included within the resolution of Mr. Pickard and Mr. Campbell.

The resolution was received with applause, but ultimately, ,at the suggestion of. one of the speakers, the motion was Carried with the exception of the latter clause, there being , oily One dissentient.

div.head: TJIE MINERS' STRRE IN LEIGH AND BOLTON .DISTRICTS.
div.p: TJIE MINERS' STRRE IN LEIGH AND BOLTON .DISTRICTS.

The resistance of the miners of these districts to the pro- posals to contract out of the Employers' Liabiality Act has occasioned surprise in many quarters, the masters in the majority of cases having concluded that little or no trouble would be experienced in persuading the men to accept their terms. The pits at which the colliers are at work are those of the Tyldesley Coal Company, Mr. W. Ramsden, and the Wharton Hall Coal Company, Tyldeslev ; and Mr. Speak- map, at Bedford. Including datallers, about 900 are thus in employment. On the other hand, the pits of 'the Astley and 'Tyldesley Coal and Salt Company, Messrs. T Fletcher and Sons, Messrs. Fletcher, Burrows, and Co.'s Atherton Collieries, Wigan Cpal and Iron Company (Westleigh), Mr. Diggle's West- leigh 'Collieries, the Bickershaw Coal Company, and the Abtam Coal Company, are all stopped, and all hands tdd will muster 7,000 men. In this estimate Hindley is not in- cluded, nor any portion of what is known as the Wigan district, except Abram. At a meetmg a few weeks ago at ,the Atherton Collieries Village Club it ,was decided by a majority to accept the employers' terms. Messrs. Fletcher, Burrows, and Co. inform our correspondent that not being anxious to put any pressure upon their miners tbey were somewhat late in submitting their proposal, and they are taken by surprise in the step which the men have now adopted, not having been made aware of what was intended until the Sl.st of December. The strike of colliers in the Bolton district is extending. Ow Thursday, conditions of employment were served on the miners Of the Clifton and Kersley Cldliery Company. They, llowever, rekeed to subscribe to thein, and so contract themselyes out of the gmployers' Liability Act, and left the pite. On Thursday. evening mass meetings were held at BdTtotroliettley,`Little Milton, and Little Lever, at which it viasvreaolved to eulhere to the determination not to con- tract out ufhe Act,, and petitions were extensively signed requelting Mr. Macdonald to endeavour to have the clauses of the Act made Compulsory. Mnfulzs' liAitowst. CONMENCE.-A special co' Isfefebee of the miners of the United Kingdom will be held in ihe Old Town Hall, Manchester, on Monday next and four or five following days. At thie meeting there will be considered manyinmortant matters in connection with mines and affec- ting miners. These will include many and important sug- gested changes in the jaw. There will also be discussed at this meeting the Employers' Liability Act," together,, as the circular states, "with the doings of men z.iclvislng to contract or having contracted out of the previsions of - the Act." The conference will be presided over by -Mr. A; Matdonald, M.P.
