Let Roman r....athollcs cease to hurl their anathemas at Protesta:-.,o;and Protestants abstain from their denouncing the P.,,,pe as Antichrist, and of the adoration of the Virgin :Lis idtilatry. And whilst we still hold our own belis,ls with most tenacious grasp, let us exhibit and en- courage that broad spirit of Christian charity which believes unfalteringly that "God is no respecter of persons. But in every nation, he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepte.d with him," and then we may hope that light will ;rise out of darkness, and that in spite of all the seeming triumph of wrong and chaes and darkness, 7:lP,,,,hteousness will triumph and a broader, fuller freedom teign. Then let us pray, that come It may. As come it will for a' that, That .ease an' worth, o'er a' the earth, May boar the gree, an' a' that. For a' that, an' a' that. It's coming yet, for a' that. That man to man the world o'er, Shall brothers be for a' that. Legislation may accomplish a great deal, but an enlightened public opinion which shall dissipate the idea that the Eng- lish and the Irish are natural foes will accomplish a great deal more, and if by our action we can do ever so little to encourage the belief that every subject of the realm has an equal interest in the maintenance of order, and that no pri- vilege that is granted to one partof the kingdom is denied to another, then we shall at least have lent our little helping hand in the accomplishment of that reform which God, in His all embracing providence has been carrying on for ages. Above everything let us not give way to craven hearted fear, and doubt the omnipotence and everlastingness of right, and truth, and justice. Although we are compelled to look upon the dish of swords in the sunlight and to admit that strife and contention seem to abound, yet the Lord reigneth, and out of all the strife and confusion there shall be born a fairer day for us and for the kingdoms of the world. I shall not stay to recount the legislative enactments of the year. Some good work has been done, and measures that frill have large influence upon the future of the country have ben passed. In so far as our Legislators, have recognised the claims of truth and Christian sentiment, we thank them for the work that they have done, and in so far as they may violate the plain and unalterable requirements of New Testa- ment Christianity, whether here, in England, or in distant places of the earth, we ought never to withhold from them our protest and our condemnation. In referring to the social aspects of 1880, some encourag- ing features present themselves to our view. Of course there is also much, that is dark, and foal, and lothsome in the social life of the people. The records of our police courts, and the,stories of crime and uncleanness with which all readers of newspapers are unhappily familiar, make it im- possible for any earnest and conscientious person to relax a single effort to win the people from sin, aud to a better and a nobler life. We must not give up hoping, believing, pray- ing, working, for the salvation of men. We must labour week tin week out from morn to night, facing all opposition bravely, and bearing it down before the force of a conse- crated love, for the aged is crying out for earnest workers and for help in the fierce battle which rages on every hand. From Babylon the mighty, for ever and for aye, Float the voices of her toilers, and the fighters in the fray; Float the voices of the victims high ab ye the battle's din, As they chant in fitful measure all the ballads of her sin. From Babylon the mighty, the monster chorus swells. A cry to one vague heaven from all the million hells; The wells of souls despairing, themarse of maddened woe, The shriek of hunted wretches dWee the the ruthleos foe. rhea the half-hushed-whisper, the growing murmur', then The deep hoarse cry foi vengeance of fierce and frenzied men, Toe wild barbaric music that crashes through the spheres, 0 die away in echoes, of the women's sobs and tears. I hear the lonely singer who wanders from the crowd, Whose song is sung in secret, with blanched face earthward bowed, Who shuns the swollen chorus and seeks this ear alone, To tell a Chid of sorrows what sorrows men had known. From Babylon the mighty, for ever and for aye, Float the voices of her toilers, and the fighters in the fray : Float the voi Ts of her viciams high above the battle's din, As they chant in fitful measure all the ballads of the sin. _

But there is no dark cloud ivithout its lining of silver sheen, and amid all the shadows that rest upon our social life tlier is here and there a rift of blue. And this is no mere utterance of a wish that is father to the thought, for the statistics of the year point to the fact that the Sabbath has not been desecrated by bacchanalian riots or drinking' orgies during the past year in any such degree as has been frequently the case in former years, Whilst pauperisen in the conntry at large, and in some districts notably, has been les- sened very appreciably. For these things we give thanks to God, and take courage. Two facts which I may mention in this connection are so full of interest and importance that I have hesitated whether to mention them as national or social questions. The effort that has been madb ,to prevent the imprisonment of young children may not have acebmplished much at present, but if by any means we can keep children of tender years free from the companionship and contagion of those who' have been steeped in crime, the influence for good upon future generations will be incalculable. Some- times the mere spirit of mischief altogether unaccompanied by any moral wrong may lead to a child's conviction, and in such a case it is bad political economy, as well as bad morality, to send a child to prison. It always has paid better to reform than merely to punish, and the reformatory, and not the gaol, is the place for all such cases as those I love referred to. The acceptance by the House of Commons and the Government of the principle of local option promises much in favour of asocial reformation of the manners and cus- toms of the people, and it onix remains now for the principle, in some form or other, to be applied in legislation in order to reveal how anxious many thousands are to shake off the weary chain of indulgence, the links of which have been f,rged by long years of evil habit, fostered and encouraged by legalised temptation. A great deal has been done towards improvement in the social life of the nation by temperance woi kers, by the diffusion of tracts treating in plain homely language upon sanitary science, and by the large increase of coffee and cocoa taverns in large towns. This ,list, indeed, is one of the most pleasing facts that I am acquainted with, and, mark you, it is in no sentimental or namby pamby style that their business is done. It is a commercial speculation as well as a moral refOrmation, and, as a general thing, it pays. Sons time ago Lord Derby gave clear testimony on thiahead. He said, "In Liverpool a coffee company has lieen set up within the last two or three years, and it is so prosperous, that when a few ;nonths ago, by way, as I thought, of giving it a lift, I wrote asking for a few shares, I found that instead of offering a favour I was asking one, for the shares had all been taken up, and stood at a high pre- mium.' Such facts are encouraging, and lam glad that in our own town this movement is extending. For if those who have been in the habit of drinking at the public-house can only be induced to visit the cocoa room or coffee tavern instead, a moral and a social revolu- tion will soon be effected. In the literary world a number of events of commanding interest have transpired ; but I can only refer to one or two out of the multitude which deserve attention. Of the making of many books there is no end and the past year has been fruitful in its produc- tions of a literary kind. From the poet laureate we have a new volume, which seems likely to sustain the splendid fame of its great author. Miss Lonsdale has written a life of Sister Dora, which is the record of a noble woman's devo- tion and heroic self-sacrifice, and which possesses an interest of a most pathetic and enduring kind. Justin M‘Carthy seems to have risen above the temptations which must always beset a strong party man, and his History of Our Own Times has secured for him an honourable place amongst the historians of this and every age. The Earl of Beaconsfield's Endymion created a great sensation, and is in its author's well-known and perhaps inimitable style; but to many people it will be chiefly valuable as showing how, amid all the cares and anxieties of State, a leading states- man of our day found time and inclination to devote himself to literature, and to write a work of fiction founded upon facts which have presented themselves to him during his experience of parliamentary life. But the one literary event of the year, which stands clear against a darkened sky which overshadows all the rest, is the death of "George Eliot." I cannot tell how much I owe of all that is best in the blood and bone and tissue of my thoughts to the woman who wrote under that 714971 cle pluthe. Many of yon, perhaps, were not at all familiar with fier works, and if this be so I must ask your forbearance while I pay a small tribute of gratitade to a writer who belonged to the entire civilised world. Ido not accept her creed of Positivism, nor do lat all largely' share her administratien of Comte; but I know of no series of boas, wiltten by One author, in which the duty of serving God by serving our fellow-men is so nobly and faithfully taught. One of the first of her books that I read was Adam Bede, and those of you who are familiar, with it will remember the sweet Methodist preacher Dinah Morris. Just before coming here to-night I read the follow- ing words, spoken in a chapter of the book to which I have just now referred: "When she came to the question, 'Will God take care of us When we die r, she uttered it in such a tone of plaintive appeal that the tearacarne to some eyes." AB I read the passage I remembered how the young woman whom George Eliot immortalised died and passed away to loin that choir whose music is the gladness of the world. I remembered that to me had been given the privilege to stand beside her grate with one who had travelled. miles with her on preaching excursions, and with another who closed her eyes when she lay dying and having a deeper interest in the writer, who embalmed her memory because of these experiences. I felt I could not allow the present opportunity to pass without laying a wreath of loving memories on her grave. George Eliot is regarded as the greatest literary genius that, ~has arisen since Shakespeare 'e days; and I have no hesitation in giving assent to such a tribute. That she was too full of sadness about the world and its inhabitants, and that her, tendencies were sometimes of a fatalistic kind no careful reader of her books can deny, but the ideal she always brought before us was a most noble one, and she always sought to inculcate a high and pure morality and a stern devotion to the welfare of the world. And now the woman who was unquestionably first amongst the intellectual and literary celebrities of the age has passed away. The turf is fresh upon the rave of the most splendid of all those geniuses who flash out light and instru.ction upon the path we tread. , That busy brain will never serve us more, the pen has dropped for ever from her band, and no more shall we meet her, except in the pages of those hooks which shall still give to thousands an inspiration which but for her they never would have had. lii the ecclesiastical world three events of more than usual interest have engaged attention during the past year. div.head: 'RUNCORN BOARD OF COM MISSIONIRS.
div.p: 'RUNCORN BOARD OF COM MISSIONIRS.

LIVELY PROCEEDINGS. The monthly Tweeting was held on Monday. Mr. George Marshall occupied the chair, and there were RISO present Messrs. Norman, Lyon, Wil!lame, Handley, Frith, Steele, Dr. McDougall, Briscoe, Shaw, P. Speakman, Meadoweroft, Linaker (law clerk), Mouritz (medical officer), Parker (Cur- Weyor), and Brookes (secretary). MEDICAL MONTHLY AND ANNUAL REPORTS. The MEDICAL ()grime presented his monthly report, which showed that the number of deaths registered in Run- corn during the month was EL Of these three were due to pulmonary diseases, three to dropsy, three to diseases of the nervous system, two to marasmus, two natural decay, and one cancer, representing a death rate of 13.10 per 1,000 per annum. Forty-eight births took place during the month, being a birth rate of 41 per 1,000 per annum. One in- quest had been held, making the total deaths 17. The setae officer presented his annual report, which stated that it afforded him much pleasure to be able a second time to con- gratulate them on the satisfactory state of the health of Runcorn. The number of deaths registered in Runcorn and Halton-with-Runcern for the past twelve months was 272, representing a death rate of 194 per 1,000 per annum. Twenty inquests had also been held, making the total deaths 292. During the year 036 births had taken place, being at the rate of 45 per 1.000 per annum. In the first quarter there had been 50 deaths, in the second 70, in the third 91, and in the fourth 61. The deaths in the first quarter were ehiefly due to disease, of the respiratory organs (24 of them being infants.) There were only three cases ot zymotic disease, resulting from diptheria. In the second quarter the deaths from diseases of the respiratory organswerc again in excess. There were two cases of fever—one enteric and the other typhoid. The infant mortality was 25. Third quarter: diarrhcea accounted for, 38; and this disease was somewhat exceptional!? prevalent. There were 59 deaths of infants, and one from enteric fever. Fourth quarter: The diseases were chiefly of the respiratory organs. There was one case of enteric fever, and 19 deaths in infant life. Each week he had inspected the meat and fish exposed in the market for sale. During the year he had condemned 700 putrid herrings, also two kincla of fish, and an amount of musty pork during the tropical summer. Eight houses which he had iespected indifferent localities he had declared Irina for human habitation, owing to insufficient accommo- dation. The district under the management of the Board was at the present time particularly healthy, and to the best of his knowledge was free from epidemic diseases. During the year there had been only one case admitted to the infectious diseases hospital. - At the request of Mr. Lyon, Mr. Barker read a statement, which showed that in 1876 the deaths (not including ire- questsl were 3C2; in 1872, 384; in 1877, 310; and in 1880, 272. Mr. LYON said that, considering the increase of the popu- lation which there had been in the town, these statements were very satisfactory. &COMPLIMENT FOR A CONTRACTOR. The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee were passed me the motion of Dr. STUELE, seconded by Mr. NORMAN. They contained the following recommendations: —That notices be served on the owners of property in Canal-street and Pennington's-row to abate nuisances. That the sewer in Bridge-street be carried up sufficiently to drain the property at the upper end of the street. That the appli- cation from Luke Cavanagh to register his house for lodgers, be refused. A letter was read from Messrs. R. Lea and Son, stating that they had no title to the land on which they proposed to erect a gunpowder store, and a resolution was passed by the committee that they declined to grant a liceuse for the premises. The Law Clerk was instructed to take such legal proceedings as he might deem necessary against the Rev. Canon Barclay and Major Orred with reference to notices served on them to abate a nuisance at the Big Pool. That, subject to the consent of the owner of the property, the footway at the corner of Waterloo-road and Church-street be reduced ir width, and that the steps of the property recently erected by Mr. Farrell, at the end of Church-street, be altered in accordance with the level of the street at the expense of the Board. Mr. NORMAN paid a high compliment to the night soil contractor for the energy and promptness with which he was carrying ont his work. THE HOSPITAL.—ONII STEP IN ADVANCE. The minutes of the Canal Boats and Hospital Committee were approved, on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. HANDLEY. It appeared from them that Mr. Dinsey, of the Local Government Board, met the committee on he Bth inst., and inspected the hospital site on the Weston-road. Instructions had been given to the Law Clerk to take im- mediate seeps for theacquisition of the land for the hospital, including the cottage and garden occupied by F.Bebbington, and the Surveyor had been asked to prepare plans for the building. AMUSING DISCUSSION ON THE FIRE BRIGADE.—FIERY WORDS BETWEE DR. M`DOUGALL AND MR. SHAW. The minutes of the General Purposes Committee con- tained a short but graphic account of the inspection of the members of the Fire Brigade. The committee had resolved that a man be engaged to clean the street lamps at 3s. per day wages. That Mr. J. Peck's tender to supply horses, when requirea, for the fire engine, at a fixed charge for a certain number of miles, be accepted. That the collector take legal proceedings against Mr. S. Ravenscroft, unless Certain conditions be complied with. That accounts amounting to £2B Os. 7d. be passed for payment. Mr. NORMAN proposed, and Mr. WILLIAMS seconded, ths adoptien of the minutes. Mr. FRITH desired to know whether the report was correct that the committee had given the members of the Fire Brigade permission to go round the town for the purpose of soliciting gifts. He could not see what business they had to go about on such a matter when they were paid for their services. Mr. NORMAN had not heard such a question raised before the committee. Mr. MEADowcaorr Perheps Mr. Frith takes exception to their going round in uniform. I think they ought not to be allowed to use the uniform except for the business of the Board Dr. McDornALL : The superintendent asked me if I had 2ny personal feeling on the matter, and I said I had not. I think they have only followed a custom which has obtained for many years. I do not think there has been any great berm done. Dr. STEELE: I do not see any reason why they should not eio so, if they wish. Mr. SnAw considered that such an expression of opinion as that given utterance to by Dr. Steele ought net to go from that Board. If the members of the Fire Brigade were justi- fied in parading the town to solicit such gifts, the scavengers, the surveyor, the solicitor, and the secretary had a perfect right to adept a similar course. (Laughter.) They ought not to give countenance to anything of the sort. Dr. STILELE We do not give our countenance to it; we say nothing about it. (Laughter.) • Mr. Fittest: You might just as well say that the Law .Clerk, the secretary, and other officials of the Board should go roand with the hat! • Mr. NORMAN (humorously): The Law Clerk is secretary now. Mr. FRITH: Yes, he has just been soliciting me. Laughter.) Mr. HANDLEY remarked that when the Fire Brigade came under the control of the Board, it was clearly understood that there were sufficient helmets for a reasonable time, reckoning those already belonging to the Commissioners and those bought from the representatives of the Volunteer Fire Brigade. He, however, saw that in the accounts passed by the committee there was one for tyre additional firemen's hats. He had no personal feeling in the matter, but he al- ways understood that whenever any purchase was made by a committee, a resolution meat be passed; and he had seen no record of such a motion. • The CHAIRMAN: Perhaps Dr. McDougall, as chairman of the committee, will answer the question. Dr. McDoroArt: I don't think I shall, unless an amend- ment is moved. Mr. SHAW : Then the best course will be to let the account go, and those gentlemen who took the responsibility of giving the order will have to pay the money out of their own pockets. Mr. LYON: In oraer to put the metier right, I beg to pro- pose that the minutes pass, with the exception of the account relating to the hats. My object is simply to keep the Board legally ri •itt.. • Mr. HANDtur : If the chairman of the committee states that the uniform was not complete without these hats, then the complexion of the matter will be altered. I know that a good deal has been said in the town in regard to the some- what prodigal expenditure of the committee in regard to the uniform they are providing for some of their officers— perhaps I ought rather to say " subordinates " (A laugh.) I am of opinion that when accounts of this kind are pre- sented, we ought to have a clear understanding why the wiPenditnre haft been incurred. Mr. FRITH said he would second the amendment as to Mr. Werrall's account for helmets, which he believed amounted toil. Dr. McDonome.: They are not helmets at all; they are
I,

rasps. Mr. Tionstaw We will embody the amendment in the .motion for the adoption of the minutes, it you like. Do you object to that ? Dr. MCDOUGALL : Certainly. Seven members voted for the amendmett and fire against it, so that it was declared
•amcd. The CIIMIIMPT said it was suggested by the Law Clerk that a're4ntution might now be put for the payment of the secount for caps. Mr. SHAW: I do not think the law clerk has any right to

augge-it. The LAW CLERK : I simply suggested Mr. Sitio, said the money had been,spent, and be did net think that the adoption of such a course as that suggested wcniki "tlefY the auditor. He considered it very important that they ahould have competency in the chairman of such a commit" t^ :conduct the business in a proper way. If chairmen of committees were not competent, the sooner they resigned the better. If the chairman of the committee did not know that his business was to pass no account without a resolution, he ought not to come before the Board and say he did not think he shoald answer a prop& question, when put in relation to the matter. pr. Mc Doroam. I beg to call the attentien of the chair- ' main v., the fact that there is no resolution before the meet- ing, and I 4SI: that the speaker shall put whatever he has to the (oral of a motion. 116;frInsavir, sitn simply stating wtat I think-- Pr. MCDOUGALL : And I have to call Mr. Shaw's attest- to the fact that there is no standing order which will permit him to pursue such a Gouria- lir. snew: Tb4quettteis beton the Board at the preweat

Dr. McDonaeLt. : There is no question before the Board at the present time. Mr. SHAW: I think that when the conduct of the com- mittee is before us, I have a right to criticise, in a simple or in an extensive form, if I choose, the conduct el the chair- man in the transaction of the business. What I said was that I thought the chairman of the committees when they bring a matter before the Board, ought to see that there is a resolution upon it. It was suggested that the motion for the confirmation of the minutes should be passed, on which Dr. MCDOUGALL said before that course was adopted he wished to make a few ob- servations. For the purpose of affording himself an op- portunity of doing so, he should move the adjournment of the Board. He protested against personal attacks on mem- bers. They heard a great deal of Mr. Shaw on that Board and outside of it, and also ef his personal vanity. (Sensation.) He must be permitted to say that it was not the business of Mr. Shaw to make personal attacks upon anx gentleman. Mr. SHAW : May I ask the Chairman to request the mem- ber to speak only of what any other member may have stated. The CLERIC: Dr. McDougall is about to move the adjourn- ment of the Board, and then you will have the chance of replying to him. Mr. Snaw : So he may do; bet I hope that this Beard will not prove to be one where gentlemen will be per- mitted to bring individual matters into this room. If Dr. McDougall wishes to do that, I am quite prepared to meet him.
Dr. McDonnell.: There is not the slightest doubt that Mr. Shaw has a perfect right to construe matters as be things proper, but he has no right to come to this Board and---

The CHAIRMAN: Speak in the third person. Doctor. Dr. McDotcoata.: He has made personal remarks about the chairman of the committee; and if it is not a personal attack I do not know what is. If he has not a proper acquaintance with the English language, I am vain enough to think that I have some little knowledge of it. Why does not he propose a resolution and at once say what he means? IL is quite evident that what he intends is to make a personal attack. The CHAIRMAN : Will you address me, Sir? Dr. McDotroeu,: lam addressing you now. I say that Mr. Shaw has made a personal attack upon an individual as to whether he is competent or incompetent; and I do not think he is an authority upon such matters. Mr. SHAW: Will you ask Dr. McDougall to discuss the question that is raised by bun? Dr. McDorroeu. : I am discussing it. Surely Mr. Shaw is not vain enough te suppose that because he takes a certain yiew of a question it is necessarily a correct one. He has a perfect right te take exception to a certain minute, but when he goes out of his way to make a personal attack upon me he is out of order, and ought to know he is so. As far as I am concerned, I fail to see that I am at all out of order, or that I have exceeded 920 10itu4e allowed to each commis- sioner. A question had been raised in regard to the bats of the members of the fire brigade. I would beg to remind some of the members that they are not helmets, as some gentlemen have stated they are; and if they bad been put down as such in the minutes, they ought not to have been. An understanding was come to that the members of the brigade should have suitable head covering. The matter was overlooked at the last committee meeting as I had to go away, and the resolution on the subject was unfortunately left out. This most undoubtedly must have escaped the memory of the secretary, or the statement would have been put upon the books that these caps had been ordered. I fail to see what advantage would be raised by sending the mem- bers about with billycocks upon their heads instead of proper head aresses. In conclusion, I beg to move the ad- journment of the Board, and I do so with very great reluctance.

The CHAIRMAN : Will anyone second the proposition? Mr. SHAW said he would second it—(laughter)—and pro- mised that he would not detain the Board long. He must, in the first, say he was of .opinion that it would have been better if the resolution had not been moved, as he did not think the subject had been made any clearer by the remarks of the Doetor. He (the speaker) was quite willing to admit that no resolution was before the meeting at the time he raised the discussion, but when two mmhers had asked questions about the affair, the chairman of the committee sat down in his plaoe and would not condescend to give any explanation. Now if anything was contemptible and dis- respectful to the Board, surely it was so for the chairman of a certain committee to treat them in a way like that. In fact, such conduct was really beyond the conception of any one who had not been a witness to it. This was the style in which Mr. Handley and Mr. Lyon were treated when the subject was brought forward. He also maintained that it was the duty of the chairman of any committee to give all possible information to the commissioners at their monthly meeting. It was not really a question of whether certain men belonging to the fire brigade should go without hats that was before them, but a matter of principle. He felt sure that the majority on the Board desired that they should not have these con- stant surcharges made upon gentlemen. Whatever else they might do, he hoped they would endeavour to discharge their duty as members of that Board to the best of their ability. They certainly could not expect perfection any- where, but he thought, at least, the chairman of a com- mittee ought to be aware whether a resolution had been passed upon a certain subject or not. Dr. McDocoam. : I quite recognise that there was not a resolution upon it. The CHAIRMAN: Do you persist in the resolution which you have moved? Do, you wish it to go to the vote or not?

Dr. McDoncum, lam entirely :in the hands of the Board. I moved the proposition so as to put rsyself in order; and I shall leave it to the Board to say whether they will negative it without a division or not. _. • _ . .

The Liternatax : Dom any gentleman wish to make any remark upon the proposition that the Board adjourn ? Dr. McDonnell.: If the motion be going to a division, I must claim the right of saying a few words. The LAW CLERK: There is nothing to which you can reply. The motion was then put and negatived unanimously, amidst laughter. Mr. LYON expressed his regret tbat the personal matter should have been introduced at the meeting, and said in order that the business might be proceeded with, he would move that the account be passed. Mr. FRITH seconded the amendment. Dr. McDouaatx : Mr. Chairman, the matter is now before the meeting, and I hope that, notwithstanding what has been said, you will consider that I have a right to make some observations upon this bill. Mr. HAlstaar : Mr. Chairman, is the doctor replying before the motion is put? The CHAIRMEN: No; he is speaking to the resolution. Mr. HANDLEY observed that be was the first gentleman to raise the question then under discussion,and he could assure the members be did not do so with any wish that the account should not be paid, for when any tradesman had supplied goods the debt thus incurred ought to be honour- ably discharged. However, he must mention that there were circumstances that fully bore oat the remarks made by Mr. Shaw. He (the speaker) was not actuated in anything he might say by any such motive as that of making an unwar- rantable attack upon the committee. He might, first of all, state that when the fire brigade were first constituted there was a sufficient number of helmets. He wasquiteaware that since that time, ostensibly with the object of establishing 50M0 memorial of Mr. Imision, the lamented head of the brigade, some £l2 10s. had been expended in bnving the old accoutrements of the organisation, amongst which were a number of helmets. He could not, therefore, understand the statement of Dr. McDougall when he referred to what he believed he had described as a scarcity of head gear for the members of the brigade. The articles referred to through- out the discussion were caps, not helmets, and he therefore came to the conclusion that the gear must be holiday gear, and not such as would be used in active service—at a fire. He hardly knew whether it would be fair to mention the matter or not, but he believed the secret history of the two caps was as follows :—One of the members of the brigade— a deputy captain—appeared at the grand review held by the chairman of the committee and one or two other members. (Loud laughter.) It was thought wise to distinguish the two superior officers of the, force, and, therefore, they were each ordered a cap—although it was known that a ehapoisit was of no use whatever for the member of a fire brigade—to distinguish them from the common men of what he might call the regiment —(laughter)—the other twelve or fourteen. Now, he did not think this expense ought to have been in- curred for the mere purpose of ornamentation, especially after the £l2 lOs had been spent for additional helmets and head-gear. Such things as these might be looked at a little more closely. In conclusion, he might say that the two chiefs had had their hats embroidered, so as to mark the superior position they occupied. Dr. McDonotat, : That has involved no additional cost. Mr. SHAW: And it is of no use whatever. The resolution in favour of the account being paid was then passed, and thn minutes of the committee were approved. TINA:NM—IN UNCOLLECTED DEBT..

The motion for the approval of the minutes of the Finance Cominittee was proposed by Mr. Lyon and seconded by Mr. Norman. They showed that the receipts for the month amounted to £578 3s. 4d., including £26 15s. Id. for market rents and tolls, £196 16a. for private improvements, and £347 Is. sd. on account of General District Rate. Instruc- tions had been given to the collector (Mr. Brookes) to make application for the ground rent due from the County Treasurer. Dr. McDorraer.s. desired to know how it was that the ground rent had not been collected for some years; it seemed a singular method of doing business. It was stated that an examination of the deeds of the commissioners by the law clerk had revealed the fact that the money ought to be paid, and if any blame were to be apportioned Mr. Brook was willing to take it. Dr. McDouoin hoped that a ledger account had been opened for the ground rent, so that in succeeding years it would not require the examination of a deed to find out that the money was legally due. The minutes were approved. THE BOARD AND THE BRINE scurnon.-11IPOR1ANT
DISCUSSION.

The CHAIRMAN said he had received an informal co.m- munication from the promoters of the scheme for bringing brine from Marbury for the purpose of making salt at Runcorn. There was no doubt if the scheme wera success- fully carried out it would increase the trade and prosperity of Runcorn very much; add to the population, and pro- bably be the of a new era in the annals of the town. He understood the company would employ about 600 men, and he thought they ought to afford the promoters every faoility for carrying out their works. Es had an idea that the board should forward a raptorial to tits Marquis of

div.p: commencement
TItI EXAMINVIL SAITTPRAI, JANUARY 8. 1181.

Cholmmdeley, urging him to meet the wishes of the emu- pany in allowing the pipes to pass through his land. lir. Chadwick, who was the Board's representative on the Weaver Trust, had asked him what the opinion of the Board was, but of course he could only tell him what his ' own opinion was—that he was decidedly in favour of the scheme, and he also remarked that he was inclined to believe the opinion of the Commissioners would be the same. Mr. NORMAN moved that a memorial be forwarded to the Marquis of Cholmondeley, as suggested by the Chairman. He thought the trade of Runcorn would be very much in- creased if the scheme were successful, Mr. HANDLEY seconded the motion. He considered the Commissioners were taking a wise step, seeing that every other Board near Northwich had thought fit to take some action. A general impression in Northwich was that their town would be seriously injured if the new scheme were I carried out, and therefore they thought it their duty to do all they could to oppose it. Runcorn ought to leave no 1 stone unturned in order to bring into the town a matter which promised to add so materially to its future welfare. The Daresbury Highway Board held their meeting on Thursday last, and he thought it would be wise to com- municate with them on the subject, as he saw that the Northwich people were intending to represent the hardship of their case at that meetirg. Mr. SHAW was of opinion that they were asked to go out- side their legitimate duty in what the Board was requested to do. There was a duty devolving upon the Board to give facilities for the proper transaction of business in the town ; but he was not aware that it was the duty of the Board to solicit in any shape any business to come into the town, or to take any responsibility. As business men, they could not subscribe to what was proposed, because they did not know what charges there might be on salt. If the Company would say they would supply salt in the town at a certain rate, which was lower than they could at present obtain it, then there would be a certainty of a benefit ; but as long as they I did not know anything about this, he did not think they had I any right to do anything whatever in making arrangements of any kind. It was a question between Lord Cholmondeley I and the promoters of the scheme. If works were erected in the town, then he was sure they would be willing to receive the promoters favourably; but it would not be a wise thing to interfere between the landowners of Northwich and Run- corn and the promoters of the scheme. He hoped the Board would not begin to go into matters which did not concern them. If they would only set themselves enquiring into their own town's matters they would find they had plenty to do, without going outside their legitimate business. There- fore he would advise them not to pass the resolution. . .

Dr. STEELE agreed with the remarks of Mr. Shaw, and if he would move an amendment to the motion he would second it. The CHAIRMAN maintained that the establishment of such works would increase the amount of traffic in Runcorn, and surely if the Board were good for anything, one of their first duties was to look after such a question. Mr. FRITH said the question was not a private one, and he should be sorry to see the day when private questions were allowed to crop up to the detriment of the public. (Hear, hear.) He.felt indignant at times when he saw what he considered attempts to place private questions in such a position. They should remember they were pledged to do the best they could for the town, and he believed if they I furthered the brine scheme, they would further the welfare of Runcorn. He suggested that a similar memorial to the one proposed to be sent to the Marquis of Cholmondeley be forwarded to the Daresbury Highway Board. Mr. SgEs.xuaw wished to know what guarantee the Board had that the works would be erected at Weston Point, even though they exerted themselves to the utmost. The LAW CLERK said the Company had bought land at I Weston Point. Mr. LYON said the action which had been taken in North. I wich showed that it was not desired to get rid of the trade, and with reference to the remarks of Dr. Steele, he did not see what objection there would be for the brine to go to Whines. If they thought they could do with half of the loaf, well, they could have it. Mr. HANDLEY advised that they should not lose sight of what had occurred once in the history of Runcorn, and that was that landowners opposed the commencement 'of the trade which was now carried on so largely in Widnes. On another occasion a firm of shipbuilders required seme land, but this was refused them; and now Liverpool felt the benefits of a large building trade, which was once offered to Run- corn.

- Mr. MEADowcnorrdid not know whether he might safely speak on the subject, but the question really for the Board to consider was, whether the scheme was not likely to im- prove the town, and whether it was for the benefit of the ratepayers. (Rear, hear.) At the present time Runcorn would do very well with increased trade. There were many idle men in the streets, and a great deal of distress in the town; and if employment could be found it would in his opinion be conferring a great boon upon those people; and the Board ought to exercise their public functions as far as possible with a view of doing public good. He had taken great interest in the question, which he considered of much importance as affecting the interests of the inhatitants.

Mr. &HAW rose to ex-plain that what he intended to argue was whether it was their duty to interfere in a matter of this kind. He did not think there could be two opinions as to the view which might be taken of its importanc3 from a business standpoint. The LAW CLERK said the reason the promoters of the scheme asked the Commissioners to take action in the matter was, because the Northwich salt manufacturers and the Weaver Trustees had been bringing to bear upon Lord Chol- I mondeley influences to lead him to refuse to grant the way- leaves which before he was favourably considering; and the promoters considered the Commissioners might legitimately I help them. Mr. NORMAN briefly referred, to the obstacles which had in the past been thrown in the way of certain branches of trade being started in the town. This was a very favour- able moment for the Commissioners to do something byway of encouragingthe new proposal. The motion was carried unanimously. The following is a copy of the memorial, and it was agreed, on the proposition of Mr. Frith seconded by Mr. W. Handley, that a similar resolution should be forwardkl to the Daresbury Highway Board and presented by two of the commissioners:—" That the Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners are informed that influence is being brought to bear upon the Marquis of Cholmondeley to prevail upon him to refuse wayleave through his Rock Savage estates near Runcorn, in order to prevent the promoters of a company called the Mersey Salt and Brine Company (Limited) from carrying out their undertaking of pumping brine from Mar- bury to Runcorn. That the establishment of salt works at Weston or Runcorn would be of immense advantage to the trade of Runcorn and district, and would tend greatly to ex- tend the limits of the town; and the Commissioners trust that the Marquis will grant every facility in his power to further the undertaking of the proposed company; and that a copy of this resolution to be forwarded to his lordship."
THE LOVE ADVENTURE OF A RUN-1
CORN INNKEEPER'S- DAVGIITER.

- _ It is not often that the inhabitants ef the somewhat dull town of Runcorn are disturbed by adventurers who are pre- pared to stake all for love; but during the week a story, based upon the tender passion. has filled the mouths of all the gossip 2T5 in that place. It seems that Mr. Blease, who is the manager, for Mr. Ditchfield, of the Royal Hotel, has a daughter who, following in the steps of her father, himself a veritable son of Anak, is tali, like the palm and, though only some fifteen summers have passed over I;er fair cheek; her charms have proved fatal to a dark-complexioned young man, of rather handsome appearance, who has for some time been in the employ of Mr. Spann, of the Mersey Hotel, which is only a short distance from the house of the beroved. There were many difficulties in the way of the courtship makis, any rapid advances, but on the principle that "though the rose have prickles, yet 'tis plucked," and that he ought to call himself no man who hath a tongue and cannot win a woman, the young man pro- ceeded with his suit. Probably he was not so innocent of the ways of womankind as might be at first sight imagined, from a look at his somewhat youthful face. Some time ago he was connected with the Warrington Borough police force, and unless they are much maligned, some of the members of that body of men are apt suitors, and able to talk to either maid or widow, should circumstances prove favourable. The intimacy was, apparently, carried on very secretly, for though at times the father of the young lady heard whispers that there was a tender feeling between his daughter and the ex-policeman, he treated such reports as idle tales. However, on Monday evening, between six and seven o'clock, Mr. Blease found that in his weak hive "A wandering wasp had crept." _ _

- The lovers finding constant parting so inconvenient, had come to the somewhat venturesome decision to unite their fortunes, apparently forgetful that though the wooer was about 26 years of age, and therefore, oug'at to have shown more wisdom, his Juliet was not even sweet sixteen. The parents were for some time in a state of complete mystifica- tion as to what had become of their daughter, but after the lapse of a shoot time, a romantic incident happened—a letter from her being found upon the staircase, in hich she stated that she had gone to Liverpool. This naturally aroused their suspicions, and it was decided to communicate with govrintendent Williamson, who, it is understood, advised *Wm to take instant measures to find where the young lady was. Early on the following morn- ing, the father went off to Warrington, whilst other friend.; were despached to Liverpool. Information had been tele- graphed to the former town as to the absence of the young man; and the enquiries made revealed the fact that on the previous night the runaways had arrived in Warrington from Norton railway station, to which they had walked from Runcorn. It was also discovered that the banns had been published at St. Paul's Church, and all the arrangements made for celebrating the nuptials on Tuesday morning. The saying that the course of true love never runs smooth was destined once more to prove true, for shortly after eight; the angry father,. accompanied by the clerk, took up their posi- tion near the church gates, and on the arrival of the happy pair, whose gladness was soon turned into weeping, the further progress of the ceremony was stopped. The young lady was taken home, and her wooer was shortly afterwards removed to Rukcorn on the serious charge of abduction. It may be as we to say at this point of our story, that if the evidence sufficient to establish such a charge be brought before the Bench, they cannot deal with the prisoner, but must sand him for trial at the Chester Assizes.

The prisoner, William Ainsworth, was brought tap at the Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday morning, before Mr. S. B. Chadwick, and charged "that he did, on the 3rd inst., unlawfully take a certaiu unmarried girl named Elizabeth Blease, of the age of fifteen years, out of the possession, and against the will of one Thomas Blease, her father." Evi- dence was briefly given by the prosecutor, who stated that his daughter was under It 3 years of age; and the magistrates renianded the prisoner until Friday morning, in order that further evidence might be obtained. Hewes admitted to bail, himself in a surety of £5O, and two sureties of £25 each. Lie was also cautioned not to have any further communication with the girl in the meantime.

Yesterday morning, on the prisoner again being brought up, before Mr. R. M. Brooke, the court was packed. Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the defence. The prisoner having been formally charged by Mr. John- son, the deputy magistrates' clerk, the prosecutor was called and said: My name is Thomas Blease,and I am the, manager of the Royal Hotel, occupied by Mr. Ditchfield, at Runcorn. I am the father of Elizabeth Blease, who was born on the 15th March, 1865. Up to the 3rd inst., my daughter lived with me, but on that day she left my house, between six andteven o'clock in the evening. She left a letter on the staircaar, and the communication is in the possession of Superintendent Williamson. In consequence of what I heard, I went to Warrington on the following morning. I found that the banns of marriage had been published in St. Paul's Church, between William Ainsworth and Elizabeth Blease—the prisoner and my daughter. I waited there a few minutes until the wedding party arrived, but, of course, I had given information previously that the proceedings were to be stopped. I then gave the prisoner in charge to the Warrington pAice..lt was certainly against my will that my daughter went away with the prisoner. I was only aware that she had been keeping company with him from hearsay. He works for Mr. Spann, who keeps the Mersey Hotel, and also a.porter stores, and his house is near 1 to the Royal.
Mr. Linker (to Mr. Johnson) You have made out nothing yet, I think. I want proof a the age. Mr. Johnson: The father swears shwas born on the 15th March 1865. . _
Mr..Linaker. : That is not evidence. Mr. Johnson • Yes it is
, Mr. Linaker: What I submit is that the age must be proved in the ordinary way—by the production of the cer- tificate.

Mr. Johnson: The swearing of the father Is quite suffi- cient without the certificate. Mr. Linaker: It is not. Mr. Johnson: I differ with you; the point hem been de- cided In a particular case. Mr. Linaker : Where the register can be got at, the certi- hcate is the most satisfactory proof of the age. Mr. Johnson: That may be one way of doing it; but this man proves that the girl was born on the 15th March, 11865.

Superiatendent Williamson: A remand will be asked for this morning. Mr. Linaker: Then you are not going on with the case! If I had known that I should not have asked a question. The Superbitendent : There are two witnesses at War- riugton who have to be summoned, and the inspector who executed the warrant and apprehended the prisoner is away at Knutsford oeseions. It is, therefore, impossible, for the case to go on. I ask that it may be adjourned until Monday next.

The Magistrate: Very well ; the case will be adjourned until Monday neat. It was agreed that the prisoner should be liberated on the same bail—himself in £5O, and Mr. John Capper and Mr. Samuel Spann, in £25 each. Mr. Johnson, after consultation with Mr. Brook, said it appeared there was an understanding, when the bail was granted on Wednesday, that the prisoner should keep away from Mr. Blease's daughter. It was only on that condition that bail could be granted. The prisoner said he was willing to be bound by such a condition;; and, the proceedings in the case then terminated:

I Prisoners were brought into the station Olt another charge, iipn the previous Thursday morning, he tal them with having been concerned in the robbery at the stores,:lud they acknowlodged their guilt.—Hayes and Wilson now adn:itted the offence; but Green denied having been near the place'. Prisoners were committed to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial.—Hayes and Wilson, two of the prisoners in the previous case, were next charged with stealing 30s. from the shop of Mr. Andrew Brown, druggist, Bridge-street.—Pro- secutor stated that on the 30th ult., he saw the bag pro- duced safe in the till of his shop, at eleven o'clock in the morning, and missed it about a quarter to six in the even- ing. He had been obliged to leave the shop several times I during the day. Amongst the money wasa new half crown. —Sergeant Walker said that from a statement made by Wilson, in the polme'station, he and Inspector Hollingworth went to a spot near Wivern place, and the lad showed him a hedge in which underneath a stone were a box and purse. In the purse was 15s. Sd. (including the new half crown), and Os. 4d. was in the box. On afterwArds charging the prisoners, Wilson said "I got upon the counter, Hayes giving me a leg-up, and I got the money." Hayes admitted this statement was true. The persons were likewise committed to the seasions on this charge.—At Knutsford Quarter Ses- sions, on Wednesday, John Alfred Hayes, Joseph Wilson, and Charles Green were indicted for breaking and entering the Co-operative Stores, and stealing the goods mentioned above. Hayes and Wilson were further indicted for stealing £1 10s., the money of Andrew Browne, at Runcorn, on Dec. 30th.—They were each sentenced to a month's hard labour and five years in a reformatory.

The SECRE:r.;:n;i;ead a letter which he had received from Messrs. Kirby and Woodcock, solicitors, Leicester, stating that with reference to the bridge slope they were waiting to hear from the railway company. This concluded the proceedings.

WIDNES POLICE corwr. MONDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. A BATCH OF DminvirAnDs.—James Walsh, labourer, for drunkenness in Widnes-road on the let Inst.; Ellen Hen- shaw, Liverpool, for drunk and disorderly conduct in Witt- road, on the same date; and William Maitland, baker, for drunkenness in Oakland-street, on the 3rd inst., were each fined ss. and costs. The cases were proved by P.C.'s Brydges, Pitt, and Evans.—William Griffiths, bricklayer, Oldham for sleeping out in Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon', works, on Sunday night, was sent to gaol seven days with hard labour. The case was proved by P.C.'s Brydges, Pitt, Evans, an Murray. ANOTHER CASE OF ALLEGED UNLAWFULLY WOUNDING. —A young man, named Peter Walton, was charged with unlawfully wounding a chemical labourer, named John White.—lt appears that on the previous Friday the com- plainant and the prisoner quarrelled whilst working together at Messrs. Sullivan's chemical works. The prisoner alleges that White ran at him with a spade, got him down on the ground, and stood over him. When he succeeded in getting up, he struck the complainant a severe blow on the jaw, ' which, it is stated, has broken it.—The Inspector of Police said the complainant was still under the care of Dr. O'Keeffe, and unable to appear.—Prisoner was accordingly remanded until Monday. TITE ALLEGED UNLAWFULLY WOUNDING AT MOSS BANE. —Hugh Conley was brought up, on remand, charged with unlawfully wounding James Gormley, at Moss Bank, under circumstances already reported.—The prisoner was com- mitted to the Quarter Sessions for trial. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. W. D. Holt. _ _ .

Tull TOPER'S L/ST.—Ann—Co—rrigan, James Ireland, Tho- mas Flanagan, Charles Flynn, Patrick Tonan, James Hughes, Bridget Mannion, and Joseph Band wereeach fined ss. and costs for drunken and disorderly conduct. The cases were proved by Sergeant Eastham, and P.C.s Strickland, Stott, Moores, Laing, and Brien.—Edward Godfrey was fined 108. and costs for a similar offence on Christmas Day, it being his 28th appearance. P.C. Laing gave evidence in the case. CIIIMKEYS oar FIRR.—For being guilty of this offence, Helen Toohey (Muspratt's-row), John Joseph Moss, John Lunt (White-street), and Patrick Kane (Sutton-street), were each fined Is. and costs. THE DOINGS OF THE GORMLEY FIMILY.—John Gorm- ley, Kate Gormley, Andrew Gormley, Bridget Gormley, and James Gormley were charged with committing wilful damage to the door and windows of the beerhouse occupied by James Doyle, to the extent of es. 4d. John and Bridget admitted the offence, and the other defendants pleaded not guilty. The evidence of the complainant, his wife, and a young man named Thomas Cowley, was to the effect that on Christmas Day, a row took place in the street where Doyle lived. Although he and his wife refrained from the slightest interference with the people concerned, several bricks, two of which were produced, were thrown through the windows by the defendants, and the door kicked in. Damage was done to the amount of 63. 4d. The evidence was of a conflicting character, and nearly all the witnesses were extremely noisy in court. The two defendants who had pleaded guilty were each fined 55., and ordered to pay the amount of the damage between them. The summonses against the other defendants were dismissed.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MFNDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman) and Mr. S. B. Chadwick.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MFNDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman) and Mr. S. B. Chadwick.

AN INTERESTING COUPLE. Stephen Mottershead was summoned by his wife, Sarah Ann Mottershead, for assault- ing her. The couple have occupied the time of the Court with their differences on several occasions during the last few months. Both are under sureties, and when the case was called upon they desired to be allowed to settle their differences themselves. Complainant was, however, ordered. to proceed with her evidence. She alleged that on the 18th ult. as she was shopping, the defendant came to her, come menced a quarrel, and struck her twice. She had no wish to press the case.—The husband, in defence, charged his wife with living in adultery, and said the disturbance had arisen owing to something which had been said about his (defendant's) chadren.—The Bench considered the defend- ant had committed the assault under great provocation. They dismissed the summons; and the Chairman strongly censured the complainant for the mode of life she was leading. Tim Putaucan AND NIS WHISKEY.—Mr. John West, of the Duke of Wellington Inn, Percival's-lane, was charged with having, on the 10th ult., sold to P.C. Bossona a ptnt of whiskey, containing 28 per cent. of water.—West ad- mitted the offence, but, in extenuation, stated that he had run out of bonded whiskey and had bought a jar from a Warrington firm. This he had diluted without first testing its strength.—The Bench said they were of opinion the de- fendant's conduct was the result of carelessness, and they only ordered him to pay a fine of 10s. and costs. A DISGRACE TO HER SEX.—Elizabeth Wareing, an old woman, the wife of a boatman, was fined ss. and costs, on the evidence of P.C. Kelly, for being drunk on Saturday night. Part of the costs included two shillings paid to two men who assisted to take the prisoner to the police station in a handcart. CAPTURE OF A GANG OF ALLEGED JUVENILE THIRY/19. Jan Alfred Hayes, Charles Green, and Joseph Wilson, all about 15 years of age, were charged with breaking into the premises of the Runcorn Co-operative society, Halton-road, and stealing 10s., 31bs. of butterine, 21bs. of corned beef, and 38 cheeks.--Mr. George Powell, manager of the .storee, said that on the 25th November, he left the place secure at about seven o'clock in the evening, and: on going there* about eight on the following mosuing, he found that I the premises had been broken into, a hole about thirteen ; inches wide having been made in the roof at the back of the I shop. A boiler was immediately under the We, and this had enabled thelads to drop into the premises easily.—Sameell Jones, a youth about 11 years, said that on the night of the 25th November, he met the prisoners near Dell bridge, and they asked him to go with them to the stores to steal money, I but he said he would not, though he afterwards consented , to keep watch whilst they entered the premises. He want with them to the place, and saw them remove a elate from the roof, and get into the building, where they remained about two minutes. When they came out, Green had some butterine in his possession ; Hayas some corned beef and checks, and Wilson the money. He (witness) had some of the corned beef. Prisoners threw the butterine into the canal.--Superintondeut Williamson said that the
whim

div.head: RUNCORN PARIRE CHURCH TEA PARTY. CANON BARCLAY ON DISESTABLISHMENT.
div.p: RUNCORN PARIRE CHURCH TEA PARTY. CANON BARCLAY ON DISESTABLISHMENT.

The annual tea party in connection with Runcorn Parish Church, was held oil Wednesday evening, at the school in Church-street, and proved very successful. The tables were presided over by Mrs. Barclay,. Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Beasley, Mrs. Bryant, Miss Booth, Mrs. Cropper, Mrs. Chorlton, Mrs. Crosby, Mrs. Gregory, Miss Imison, Mrs. Joule, Mrs. Knowles, Mrs. Lightburn, Mrs. Meadowcroft, Miss R. Rigby, Mrs. Savage, Mrs. Statham, Mrs. Tonks, and Mrs. Whittaker. Donations were given by Mr. Acton, Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., Mr. Eccles, Mr. Briscoe, Mr. Hampson, Mrs. Jones, Mrsl Leicester' Dr. McDougall, Mrs. Marwood, Mrs. Massey, Mrs. Mouritz, Mr. Oldbury, Miss Rougier, Mr. B. Rigby, and Mrs. Steele.

The Chairman in opening the proceedings, delivered I a somewhat lengthy speech. He first referred to the fact that the National School Band had collapsed—not for want i of instruments, but from a want of instrumentalists. (Laughter.) There was evidently a scarcity of young men who had "music in their souls." (Renewed laughter.) They did not see the members of the choir with them that everting. This was not owing to the fact that the associa- tion had also collapsed, but they no doubt felt that their work was of too important a character—of too recherche a kind—to allow them to trouble themselves with such com- mon things as ballads or part songs! The result was that night he was compelled to almost entirely depend upon the services of outsiders, who did not exactly belong to the Parish Church, but were kind enough to come amongst them and give their services. After remarking that in each twelve months death claimed some one as his victim, and that they missed Lieutenant Garrat very much indeed, he referred to the good work which was being done in the school. Mr. Barclay made a brief reference to the establishment of a dividing club in connection with the Parish Church, and which was carried on with proper tables of payment; he said that one of the reasons alleged against some of the dividing clubs in the town was 'that they were held at public-houses. Now, he did not at all join the crusade against public-houses or those who kept them; because he believed such places to be a necessity in the present state of society; and he could testify from his , own experience that those who had charge of them were as good citizens and Christians as those who are engaged in any other department of labour. At the same time it was important that there should be a club where there was no temptation to drink. The club was opened on the previous Monday evening, and no fewer than 60 young men joined. By the next meeting they were anticipating there would be no fewer than 100 members. (Applause.) 'He could not remember any year in which the work con- nected with the church had been so satisfactorily done. r There were kw churches where they would find two chnsch- wardens and two sidesmen so regular in their attendance as their own were. (Applause.) He felt very thankful—and he thought they must all feel very thankful too—that after the excitement of the past year in Church matters, so much peace and harmony had prevailed in that parish. They heard of certain parsons doing that which their congrega- tions disapproved; of parishes where cantankerous parishoners made foolish complaints—or rather, not the parishoners themselves, for a great deal of the persecu- ticn of which they heard and read had not arisen from parishoners, but from persons edged-on by others, in .order to make a bother. At the same time, he must express his own conviction that two things had occurred during the twelvemonths —though there had been many things to en- coruage them—which he thought were taking a very con- siderable stride to what he feared they must ultimately look, viz, the disestablishment of the Church of England. He was not going to treat them to a dissertation on the advan- tages of disestablishment. He thought it was a great ad- vantage to each parish to have in it an educated gentleman who was ready to take up matters which nobody else could, perhaps, take up; and it would be a an evil day for the parishes when such a gentleman was withdrawn from them. In the course of:his decanal and ruridecanal duties, and in his visits to friends, he saw a great deal of the working of country parishes; and the thought had often struck him, what would become of such places when the clergyman, who was often doing what there was nobody else to do, not merely from a moral and spiritual, but from a temporal point 'of view, was withdrawn as the ecclesiastical head of the parish. Whew a clergyman was put in charge of a parish, living in a parsonage in the midst ol his people, there was always some one at hand to whom everybody, high and low, could appeal for advice, for the purpose of starting a variety of useful movements affecting the temporal and spiritual objects of the parishoners. Entertaining such views as he did—though he knew there were many who differed from him —of the advantages of an Established Church, he !could not but regret that two things had occurred during the current year. which, to his mind, went a long way towards promoting disestablishment. One was the Burials Bill, but in respect to that measure he must say he did not at all coincide with the views enter- tained by certain of his brethren in regard to it. He con- sidered it was inevitable when a Liberal Ministry was returned to the House of Commons by a largo majority that 1 they should feel compelled to take action en the matter, in order to'fulfil the pledges their supporters had given at the hustings. He was of opinion that Churchmen might be very thankful that the bill was entrusted to such a good Churchman as Lord Solhorne, who was himself for many years a Sunday school teacher. (Loud ,applause.) The passing of that bill was not half so bad a sign as the result , of recent triumphs. Some short time ago he had spoken in the church on this question, and tried to express, as clearly as he could, to the people present, what were his own views on the subject; and without sympathising at all with those gentlemen who, in consequence of what they might call a high ritual, had incurred the discrxlit of the law, he thought it was very hard lines that a man should b&sent to prison,' or treated like a common felon, because her, wore a garment too much, or had a candle too I many in his church. It was quite right that I there should be law, and that people should be obedient to the law; but it was nevertheless, very hard that through a mistake which Lord Brougham made in constituting the Court of Appeal, there should be such a punishment as im- prisonment. (Applause.) He must confess that it was very hard. A man might violate the law in a variety of ways; for instance, he might omit a creed, and they heard occasionally of people omiting a creed. which the Rubric distinctly said they must read, but nothing was seen of this, and the person was allowed to go scot free. They heard of another man getting up in his pulpit and saying that he did not believe this of that canonical book was irr. spired ; but if a man had a garment too much, or a candle too many,—theugh it might be very foolish—it seemed very hard that the latter should be sent to-prison and the congre- gation broken up, whereas the other men were allowed to go free. Members and ministers of the Church of England said that if this was to go on,the sooner they were disestab- lished the better! He did not at all fear disestablishment from the attacks of those who were without—they might attack them as hard as they liked but he did feel that it was a very dangerous matter when,he would not say there was treason, but dissatisfaction, in the camp, and when people, who were not extreme either way,—good old-fashioned Churchmen—were becoming discontented with the position in which they were placed as members of the Establishment, and said it could not be tolerated I When he heard of all these things he felt thankful, and returned his hearty thanks to those present for the kindly forbearance with which they received everything that the authorities of that church, both temporal and spiritual, introduced. He was net aware that they introduced any innovations. They tried to make their services as attractive as possible, and, in doing this, he had always been warmly seconded. The speaker concluded with a sympathetic reference to the death of Mr. Hartley, and moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Crosby, charchwardens, and Mr. Briscoe and Mr. Whit- taker, the sidesmen.

Mi. John Brundrit, J.P., and the Rev. J. J. Bryant, Wright-Williams (Vicar of Widnes), G. Simpson, and W. Preston afterwards delivered short addresses. During•the evening a number of votes of thanks were passed, and the proceedings were enlivened by the per- formances of the Parish Church bell ringers and songs by several friends.

THR END OE A DUTTON L.!CENSED VICTUALLERS' DINNER. —Mr. James Peck, cab and car' proprietor, sued Mr. Richd. 17.0wles, of the New Inn, High-street, !er £32 12s. 6d., being the aineunt of damage to a horse and eic,?s whilst in the defendant's charge, the loss of hire sustained, mil the charge for the use of the conveyance and horse.—Mr. Lake (Meisre. Day and Lake) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Fletchef, of Northwich, for the defendant.--Mr. Lake briefly opened the case and said the defendant hired the horse and drag on the 27t1; September last, and they were supplied on the fol- lowing day, for the purpose of going to Dutton. Whilst coming from that place in the evening the horse anid drag came into collision with a miller's lorry, and both the con- veyance and the horse were seriously damaged. Mr. Lake concluded by briefly referring to the law of contract in regard to the returning of a horse and trap to the owner under such circumstaeces. The particulars of the claim were as follow: damage to horse, £10; loss of time to horse during sickness, £5; veterinary surgeon's charges, a 125. 6d.; coachbuilder's charges, £l4, horse taking drag to Warrington, 10s. • and horse bringing drag from, Warring- ton, 10s.—The plaintiff was then called, and said the defendant saw him on the 27th September last, and he wanted a drag and a particular horse called " Mango " on the following day. He rather objected to letting the defen- dant have the horse at the first, but consented to do, so on his promising to take every care of it and not over-drive it. The horse and drag were sent to defendant's house on the following day. In the evening, on going to his stables, he found that the horse had come home nithout the drag; that it was very much damaged on the near hind leg. He gave orders that the leg should be fomented, and Mr. Baker, veterinary surgeon, of Halton, was sent for. The animal was attended for three weeks. On the following morning he went to defendant and asked if he wished to examine the drag as to the damage caused to. it before he sent it to be repaired. He paid £l4 for the repairing of the drag. The horse was damaged in one of its legs, so that if it came to be sold it would not fetch as much by £lO. He claimed £5 foe loss of the use of the horse and drag. He had paid the veterinary sargeon £2 12s. ed.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Fletcher, the plaintiff said he gave £6 ss. for the drag in February last year. He paid £5 14s. 6d. in April last for re-painting and putting in new felloes. He gave £l5 for the horse, which he took out of grass, and it improved so much under his care that he would not have sold it for £3O. The animal had formerly been a hunter, and had been injured in jumping a fence.- -Wm. Thomas Peck, son of the plaintiff, was called, and stated that he accompanied defendant to Dutton, and drove another man, but he admitted that though near the con- veyance at the time of the accident, he did not witness the collision.--Samuel Hunt, tearnsman said that onthe even- ing of the 28th September he was driving a lurry and four horses from Runcorn to Frodsham Bridge. At Halton Brook he met a horse and trap, which ran past the front of the lurry. At the same time he heard a crash,and saw a second ' trap opposite his first horse. As soon as he bad got clear of Ithe trap which was near his first horse, he returned on the road, and saw there had been a collision by which one of the traps had been broken. He asked what was amiss, when one of the company said, "Oh, we don't know the conse- quence of this yet," and he went on his without making any further enquiries.---Mr, Frederick George Baker, veterinary surgeon, gave a description of the injury sustained by the horse, which, he said, was worth £3O previous to the date of the accident. It was now worth from £l5 to £2o. David Farrell, foreman in the employ of Mr. Connor, coach- builder, Warrington, said the cost at the repairs to the drag were £l3 10,.—Mr. Fletcher respectfully submitted to the court that the very essence of the case was that actual negligence should be proved on the part of his client.—His Honour remarked that this was what he hinted to Mr. Lake at the comencetnent of the case. There was apparently no proof that the defendant did not take every care in driving. He could not take the acci- dent alone as evidence of want of care. There was no account given of the accident beyond what the teamster said, and he did not see it occur. That particular witness, when trying to explain the matter, said he thought that either the horse shied, or the driver believed he had got past the lurry, and turned into the middle of thetoad too soon. Mr. Peck's son gave a bit of evidence which seemed to show that none of the people in the case were driving fast. He said that Mango was a quick going horse, yet that his (witness's) trap was about a mile ahead of Mango at the start. This seemed to show that the defendant was not driving the horse at any great speed. Defendant had a good reputation as a,driver, and had driven the animal twice before, when it had come home all right. He did not think there was anything in the case to support the action against the defendant. There would be judgment for the plaintiff as regarded the 9s. claimed for the hire of the drag, and judgment for defen- dant as to the claim for negligence, with costs.

On Tuesday evening last a public tea meeting was held in the Bicker- staffe-street schoolroom under the auspices of the Great Heart (Lodge 2363). ;bout 70 persons sat down to an ex- cellent tea kindly presided over by Mrs. Gore, Mrs. Wheeler, Mrs. Bennett, Mrs. Skaife, and Miss Mannon. After tea the chair was ably filled by Bro. R. Williams, D.C.T., of Liverpool, and a miscellaneous entertainment was given, PARR FRIENDLY' SOCIETY, ST. HELENS. —The tenth annual tea party in connection with this society was held ,on Friday evening, in St. Peter's school, Parr. There were about 250 present. A meeting was held after the tea pre- 'sided over by the Rev. A. A. Nunn, and a programme con- sisting of readings, glees, songs catches, dm., was gone through, the following persons taking part :—Miss Lewis, Messrs. Salisbury, Saxon, Williams, P. Smith, and Millington. An address was given by the Rev. M. Sweetnam. Mr. A. Kay presided at the piano forte. The society has a mem- bership of 163, and is worth £474 4s. id. CONCERT AT SICELMERSDALE.—A concert was given in the new Market Hall, Skelmersdale, on Monday evening last, by the choir of the Catholic Church of that town, assisted by the following principals:—Miss Swift, R.A.M., (principal soprano of Holy Cross Church, St. Helens) ; Mr. Lepp, (principal tenor of Holy Cross Church, St. Helens) •, Mr. Ramsay (of Liverpool); Mr. G. Ashcroft, (Organist of St. Anne's, Sutton,) accompanist, and Mr. James Unsworth (Organist and choir-master of Holy Cross Church, St. Helens) conductor. There was a large attendance. Part first consisted entirely of selections from Handel's famous Christmas Oratorio "The Messiah." The following is the list :---Tenor (A) "Comfort ye," (B) "And every valley." Mr. Lepp; Chorus, "And the glory of the Lord," Alto," 0 Thou that tellest," Miss Jackson • Bass, ''Woy do the nations," Revd. W. Stirzaker ; Chorus, " LNt up your heads "; Treble, " Rejoice greatly," Miss Swift ; Chorus, " Hallelujah." After an interval of ten minutes the second part, composed of miscellaneous music, was gone through. The various items were :—Song by the Revd. W. Stirzaker ; "The music of the sea," Miss Hulme and Miss Rogerson; "A country life for me," Mr. Ramsay; "Blow, blow thou winter wind," Revd. JNixon ; "I'm a merry Zingari," Miss swift; "Good bye sweetheart," Mr. Lepp ; "Two merry mountain maids," Miss Swift and Miss Jackson ; " A thousand a year," Revd. W. Stirzaker ; sorig by Miss Jack- son; " The respectable man," Mr. Ramsay. There were several encores and an excellent concert was brought to a close about half past ten. TEE Sr. HELENS LIBERALS AND GOVERNMENT PEN- -510153.—The following petition, which has already annexed to it a large number of signatures, has been lying during the past week at the Liberal Club, and will soon be for- warded to Parliament :—" To the Honourable the Commons of Great Britain and Ireland in Parliament assembled.—The humble petition of the undersigned sheweth that there are several perpetual pensions of large amount now charged upon the consolidated fund annually voted by your honour- able House: that some of the said several pensions have been paid for the past two hundred years: that in some cases the origin of such said several pensions has been en- tirely unconnected with any benefit or service to the nation : that in every such instance of perpetual pension the amount already paid has far exceeded the value of any service alleged to have been rendered to the nation by the original grantee: that in some cases' the conduct of the original grantee of such pensions has been the reverse of meritorious, and the original grants of such pensions are utterly indefen- sible on any ground of public policy: your petitioners there- fore pray that your honourable House will direct careful enquiry to be made into the circumstances of the original grants of all perpetual pensions now paid, whether or not such pensions are charged on the consolidated fund, and also as to the circumstances under which each of such pen- sions is now paid, and by whom, and why, each of such Pensions has been received from the date of the original grant (when the recipients of any of such pensions are not the direct heirs of the bodies of the original grantees), and that your honourable House will, where necessary, repeal any statute and will cease to pass any vote under which such pensions are respectively payable." THE RUNCORN PROPERTY AND INVESTMENT CO., LIMITED, are prepared to receive Deposits as under :—On sums at one month's notice, 4 Pedent. per annum ; on sums at three months' notice, at 5 per Cent. per annum. Interest payable half-yearly, on the 24th June and the 24th December. The security to investors consists of the valuable freehold estates and properties owned by the CromPany, proper- ties in mortgage to the Compiny, and the large margin of mu- called capital. Deposits can be paid at any timeto Mr. James Pritchard, Leinster-read ; Mr. William Handley. Chweh- street ; and at Bethesda Schoolroom, on the first Thursday in every month, from 7-30 to 8-30 p.m.

MAKINSON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received, hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Afakinson having had from early youth practical experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himselt on a large scale; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWRIGHT busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice in Valuing and Selling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing and Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-in- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases involving Damage and Trespass. Mr. WILCOCK, also, has had the advantage of being brought up to Farming, together with that of having served an appren- ticeship to an eminent Veterinary Surgeon, combined with the experience he has had since his connection with this firm, enables him to give judicious and valuable advice in all cases in which he may be consulted. In conclusion, M. and W. beg their friends and the public generally to note that they have a trustworthy and efficient staff of assistants in their employ, who have been carefully trained to watch over the interests of those who favour the Arm with their patronage; whilst last, but not least, their system of advertising, and the facilities they possess of ensuring an extensive circulation, enable them to offer the utmost pos- sible publicity to any sales entrusted to their management.

ateredness of the hour of bereavement remains unviolated. And now any Noncomformist may have that minister and that form of service which best euita his desires, none law- fully daring to make him afraid. The appointment of the Rev. J. C. Ryle, as first Bishop of Liverpool, is an event of quite sufficient interest and importance to warrant a reference to it in any review of the year. And this is especially so in a town which forms a part of the new Diocese, and if the same interest in the welfare of men and the same devotion to work is manifested in the Bishop as so frequently revealed itself in the parish clergyman, not only Liverpool but the whole neighbourhood will feel the benefit of the appointmeat. The last event cor rather series of events to which I shall refer, is the prosecution and imprisonment of the Ritualistic Clergymen, for violation of ecclesiastical law. It is very I necessary to draw a distinction between the imprisonment for conscience sake of our forefathers, and the new sort of martyrdom which has come in vogue. Our ancestors went to prison and sometimes even to death rather than violate their conscience, but it seems to me that in the present day the penalty is paid by men who have no conscience. Tney are in no worse position than any minister would be whether Episcopalian or Nonconformist, who persiSted in violating a plainly declared law. If a Congregational or Baptist, or Wesleyan minister, persisted in violating an agreement into which he bad entered with an ecclesiastical community, lie would render himself liable to precisely the same treatment. To play the heroic martyr in such a cause is indeed to descend from the sublime to the ridiculous. My review of the year, which has of necessity been brief and cursory, is ended. And it only remains for me now to remind you that the year 1880, with all its multitude of events, brought very much of blessing to every one of you. You ought to be the wiser, nobler, purer for all that has happened during the past year, and to go forth to the duties of the present and the future with unconquerable energy and, sublime resolve, determined that in the strength of Christ, and by the blessing of God, you will live well the one brief life which God has given you to live, the little gleam of time 'twist two eternities, which once neglected may leave no other chance to you for evermore. And then, when you are called to take the sacrament of the dust, and to leave the world which'you have tried to make a better place, you shall join the Immortal dead who still live on In minds made better by their presence; live In pulses stirred to generosity In deeds of daring rectitude; in scorn For miserable aims that end with self; In thoughts sublime that pierce the night like stars, And with their mild persistence urge man's search To vaster issues.
